full_text: U.S. President Donald Trump sits at a table monitoring military operations against Iran during Operation Epic Fury on March 2, 2026. (Photo by the White House via X account/ Anadolu via Getty Images) Soon after the 2024 election, I published an article titled “ How Donald Trump Could Succeed: Or, More Likely, Fail .” I think that clearly, as of late September 2026, he is failing. The once-vaunted “ vibe shift ” has evaporated and young voters have swung back to the left. We have a House incumbent in a Trump +15 district distancing herself from Trump’s immigration policy . The big question of the midterms is whether Democrats can win Senate races in Iowa, Texas, Alaska, and Kansas — states that should not be in play. This doesn’t mean that MAGA is down for the count, by any means. The Republicans have a daunting cash advantage and the Senate math is objectively very difficult for Dems. But Trump is undeniably unpopular. And in terms of the scale of his failure, it’s worth reflecting on the fact that Republicans’ best electoral news is just that while Democrats have good nominees in a number of well-chosen races, the national party leadership has not moved to the center since 2024 and a lot of blue state progressives are being replaced by even-further-left politicians. That’s keeping Republicans in the game, to an extent. But it also underscores the reality that Trump is doing the opposite of crushing and discrediting the left — he’s rocket fuel for thermostatic counter-mobilization, just like he was back in the “ Woke 1 ” days. So if Trump has failed, how does my own diagnosis hold up? I think the answer is that it’s pretty good, but not perfect. My most successful, most fundamental forecast, one that I think a lot of tech industry people might have benefited from listening to, was that Trump was more likely to fail than succeed. Something about the Silicon Valley fast-follower mindset seems to make these guys struggle to understand the basic nature of the political pendulum, and a lot of folks like Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos who used to have more progressive personas bought high on MAGA right after Trump won, when they should have hedged their bets. Presidents usually overreach, and Trump is certainly not a person of above-average discipline or judgment. Bad luck or bad policy? One thing I noted in the piece was that despite Trump’s anti-war rhetoric on the campaign trail, the national security team he announced shortly after the election was “an extremely hawkish group that screams ‘hot war with Iran.’” In retrospect, I wish I’d made a bigger deal about this. I noted at the time that it seemed like a team that would lead the country into war with Iran and then hedged with the observation that presidents sometimes surprise us. So far so good! What I didn’t do in the piece was dwell on the idea at any length, which is too bad because I was right about the team of super-hawks and this seems to have kind of wrecked Trump’s presidency. I mentioned this back in April, but there’s a weird finding in the economics literature that Democratic Party presidents enjoy systematically better economic performance even though they don’t pursue systematically better economic policy. The explanation, according to Alan Blinder and Mark Watson , is that “the Democratic edge stems mainly from more benign oil shocks, superior total-factor-productivity (T.F.P.) performance, a more favorable international environment, and perhaps more optimistic consumer expectations about the near-term future.” They seem to primarily understand this as a question of good luck. But having watched both the George W. Bush and second Trump presidencies unfold, I think it’s because Republicans have systematically bad foreign policy that is inattentive to the downside risk of saber-rattling and hawkishness. Trump made a great show of breaking with the Bush-era “neocons” over their idealistic invocations of democracy-promotion. But the actual problem with Bush-era foreign policy wasn’t belief in democracy; it was excessive belief in the potential upside of coercive military force. Trump has retained the error while reconfiguring the goals. Overreaching on immigration In the piece , I also argued that “nothing did more to drive support for Trump than backlash to the multi-year span of chaos at the southern border due to widespread exploitation of asylum loopholes,” which gave Trump a huge opportunity to reap a political win by forcefully doing what voters wanted and shutting down the irregular inflow of unselected immigrants. He did that, and I think it’s worked well for him. I also said he’d be tempted to try to actually deliver on the promise of “mass deportation” from the interior and that this would probably generate backlash. My view was that the most prudent course would be to return to the Obama administration’s first-term policy of rapid-fire jailhouse pickups of illegal immigrants arrested for non-immigration crimes in cooperative jurisdictions and to try and avoid picking other fights. Trump has done plenty of that style of immigration enforcement, but he’s also done a lot of more aggressive interior-enforcement actions of the sort that I thought would spark mass public backlash. They kind of have, but my read of the evidence is that it’s much less backlash than I would have hoped and much less than a lot of progressives seem to believe has actually occurred — Trump’s immigration approval rating has drifted down, but it’s significantly higher than his overall approval rating or approval on any other major issue. Or to put it another way, the really clear backlash has been to extreme forms of overreach — such as immigration officials literally killing American citizens without cause and the White House covering for them. That’s incredibly bleak and it did generate, eventually, some pullback from the administration. But they’ve really gone quite far on immigration issues. Interior enforcement has been consistently aggressive, they are stripping as many people as possible of legal status , they’ve deported a considerable number of people erroneously, they’re messing up skilled legal immigration — and I think it’s hard to argue that they’re paying a big price. This dynamic is bad for Trump in a handful of South Florida and South Texas districts that are heavily Latino but swung heavily to the right in the 2020 and 2024 cycles, so it’s not like there’s zero backlash. But still, immigration is consistently one of Trump’s best-performing issues, so he’s kind of incentivized to do cruel, flashy things to drive attention to it and away from the core affordability questions that are crushing him. Moving backward on affordability I noted in the piece that the most obvious way Trump could fail would be by trying to actually implement his campaign promises on tariffs, since they directly contradicted the mass public’s urgent desire for cheaper stuff. “ Trump’s supporters in the business community say that he’s just lying and won’t do this,” I wrote , “that he’ll use the threat of tariffs to coerce certain policy concessions out of certain foreign countries.” I thought threatening tariffs and then calling off trade wars in exchange for minor, superficial, or even totally fake concessions was a pretty good idea given how much Trump himself dominates the MAGA information space. The risk to his presidency was that he’d really do it. Subscribe now Trump very early in his administration did the huge Liberation Day tariffs, faced massive market and political blowback, and backed down. But ever since backing down, he’s been trying to recreate Liberation Day in the aggregate while minimizing stock market blowback. In terms of the problem Trump is trying to solve, this has worked. Notably, the data center industry has gotten exemptions so that the construction boom is going on unabated. But this does not help people with the cost of living. In fact, the furious pace of A.I.-related investment is raising the price of consumer electronics that compete for the same stuff. Meanwhile, the tariffs as such are not having that large an impact on the overall cost of living. But in political terms, they’re a salient and obvious example of a president who was elected on a promise of lower prices acting to make prices higher. I said in the piece that it was “basically inconceivable” that Trump would avoid the kind of deficit-financed regressive tax cut that added inflationary pressure to the economy and pushed up interest rates and, indeed, that’s exactly what Trump did. So we have not only the war spiking energy prices but also Trump’s two most high-profile economic initiatives — the One Big Beautiful Bill and the tariffs — both pushing up the cost of living. It’s honestly incredibly stupid to win an election on the basis of making an impossible promise of lower consumer prices and then to take deliberate policy actions that go in the other direction. But here we are. A cautionary tale, not a model I don’t want to claim oracular wisdom on any of this, but I do think the general tenor of my forecast — that Trump would probably overreach across a broad range of issues and spark significant backlash — was basically borne out and a lot closer to the mark than once-widespread speculations about a vibe shift or a realignment. The immigration backlash point proved, I think, to be further away than I thought it was, which still didn’t stop Trump from going too far. The immigration case is a particularly pointed illustration of why I find it disturbing that so many progressive policy entrepreneurs continue to cast Trump’s approach as a model to emulate rather than as a cautionary tale. I do understand the appeal of heavily relying on legal creativity and aggressive assertions of executive power as the main mode of policymaking. The alternative is to focus on winning supermajorities , which requires a more moderate big-tent approach or else relying on bipartisan legislation as the main mode of policy change. But even on immigration, where Trump had the public squarely on his side and he acted with maximum aggression and got away with more than I thought he would in terms of public opinion, he hasn’t actually enacted any permanent legislative change . I’ve seen conservatives on social media jumping up and down with delight about Trump enacting a new “public charge” regulation for visa issuance that reverses the Biden administration’s reversal of conservatives’ prior effort to enact this regulation in Trump’s first term. This kind of see-sawing is inherently less impactful than a push to change actual immigration law would be. But to change the statutes governing who gets visas and the terms by which foreign-born people or residents of mixed-status families can access the social safety net would require Republicans to set priorities and to give Democrats some wins on topics that Republicans have decided are lower priority. By insisting on purism, you find yourself limited to executive actions and you actually achieve less. And it seems to me that as progressive schemers plot their agenda for 2029, they are basically aiming to recapitulate these mistakes. The reason Trump didn’t genuinely focus on reducing the macroeconomic drivers of high prices and high interest rates is that doing so would have required sidelining his pre-baked ideas around taxes. Democrats, similarly, will face a choice between doing internal coalition management by rebranding a progressive-interest-group agenda as “affordability” and actually focusing on affordability . And then on the broad suite of other agenda items, they will face the same tradeoff between purity-maxxing through executive action and the annoying — but ultimately more impactful — process of securing durable base hits through bipartisan legislation. If you want to reshape the country in more profound ways than that, you need some combination of winning huge congressional majorities and/or being popular enough to survive midterm backlash cycles, either of which requires being way more prudent and disciplined than Trump was rather than plowing ahead like a bull in a china shop. If you want to find a Republican model to emulate, I would forget Trump and look at New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte, who is cruising to re-election in a state Kamala Harris won despite a terrible national political climate. Notably, she pulled this off without being a Phil Scott type who’s checked by a Democratic supermajority in the legislature. There’s a red trifecta in New Hampshire, and they have chosen to behave in a disciplined way — they refused to do a MAGA gerrymander of the House map, for example, to avoid nationalizing state politics — and have made incremental policy gains and built power. I often hear that it’s impossible for political coalitions to be disciplined in the social media era, but while I agree that it’s hard, I think this is learned helplessness. They’re disciplined in New Hampshire. Trump and the Republicans have been very disciplined about abortion, while they’ve chosen to be reckless in other areas and are paying the price. Democrats shouldn’t try to harness that same recklessness to progressive ends; they should learn to behave more prudently. Share

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology has released a report on the use of A.I. in education. (Photo by Owen Franken via Getty Images) Half a million K-8 public-school students in New York City will be banned from using generative artificial intelligence this school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Wednesday. Meanwhile, students at Arizona State University will spend the year completing A.I.-driven job-integrated coursework after the university’s vice provost for academic innovation reasoned that “work must live inside the curriculum, not at the end of it.” Williams College, an elite, private liberal-arts college in Massachusetts, has outlined that while A.I. can be useful in some contexts, it should not be used by students unless instructors provide explicit permission. As rapidly developing generative A.I. technology throws the future of education into tumult, leaders at every level of student oversight are considering how to mitigate chaos and preserve the value of education. These approaches — Mamdani’s for N.Y.C. public-school students, A.S.U.’s for university students, and Williams’s for liberal-arts college students — respond to identical technology differently. Even as these three institutions go in different directions, each is plausibly making the choice most appropriate for their own specific value proposition. A.I. shrinks the gap that has historically separated students who learned from students who appeared to learn — the students whose work was traceable proof of their struggle to complete it versus the ones who found shortcuts to produce their end result. With the disappearance of that friction via tools that can do the difficult work adequately, educational leaders at every level are forced to reconsider and reckon with what exactly their institutions’ purpose is and with whether A.I. makes that proposition more valuable or undermines it entirely. Last month, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology published its committee report on “A.I. use in teaching, learning, and research training,” which is arguably the most exhaustive institutional self-examination on the subject to this point. M.I.T., a leader in both A.I. development and use, has produced a master key that, far beyond acting as a single elite institution’s one-size-fits-all prescription for all educators, is a thorough accounting of every value an educational institution could be organized around and the ways A.I.’s integration can advance or undermine the stated goal. A.I. is not creating new purposes for institutions or for education on the whole. Instead, A.I. is forcing every institution at every level of education to confront the question of what its purpose actually is. The breaking point Before 2022, which, with the release of ChatGPT, is the year M.I.T. pinpoints as the birth of generative A.I., an institution’s purpose could be implicit, avoiding much scrutiny. Lectures, problem sets, and exams all served multiple purposes, such as transmitting content, building discipline, developing judgment, performing effort, and producing a grade. Generative A.I. explodes that bundle of purposes. Students can produce passable assignments — essays, proofs, pieces of code — without actually doing the assignment and certainly without fulfilling the assignment’s theoretical purpose. In other words, it is now possible for students to produce a product without learning. Today, educators are forced to answer not whether students should use A.I., but what the point of this assignment — this education — is and whether A.I. helps or negates that purpose. M.I.T.’s report calls this question “backward design.” Educators, the university argues, ought to start with a clear view of what they want students to know or become and then work out whether A.I. supports or undermines that goal. The report is useful for educators across the spectrum (from elementary school through graduate school) as a reference frame for thinking through the issue of A.I. in education because M.I.T. is not a single kind of institution. It combines several major functions of higher education within a single university. Like other elite private schools, it is a residential college built around mentorship and the campus experience. But it is also a pre-professional training ground where students learn hard skills. It is a research university whose apprenticeship model is meant to produce future generations of researchers, and it is, not incidentally, a leader in both building and assessing the technology in question. M.I.T. has the task of evaluating how to preserve several competing value systems at once. The report’s eight guiding principles — humility, boldness, centering humanity, leaning into learning, teaching with intentionality, rejecting a one-size-fits-all approach, “augmentation not automation,” and thinking beyond the classroom and the campus — are broad enough to map onto educational institutions across a wide spectrum of purposes, such as professional preparation or community. Other institutions do not have to approach their valuation as holistically, as their choices can be read as narrower applications of M.I.T.’s report. They are special cases under the umbrella of purposes that M.I.T. defines. The special cases Public K-12 systems are designed to produce in students the basic cognitive capacity to read, think, reason, and work through problems independently. That purpose is the exact thing that unsupervised A.I. use is best at overriding in a young person’s development. It takes away the struggle necessary to grow both intelligence and confidence. New York City’s response, then, is an attempt to preserve the identified purpose of a child’s foundational education. It is also why this restrictive approach to A.I. is totally different from M.I.T.’s nuanced, course-by-course philosophy. But the N.Y.C. approach still answers the underlying question about purpose in the way that M.I.T. would if it taught eight-year-olds: One of the university’s guiding principles, “leaning into learning,” asserts that “the process of education is necessarily a productive struggle and that the most important product of [students’] education is not a G.P.A. or a diploma but themselves : their personal growth and intellectual maturity and the development of their own imagination, insight, and judgment.” For a child, developing the ability to struggle productively is the entire point of school, making A.I., by M.I.T.’s estimate, a threat to the purpose. Community college and vocational programs sit at the opposite end of the A.I.-use spectrum from K-8 education. Their credentials are meant to certify competency in a particular occupation, likely one that itself will be transformed by technology. Miami Dade College, which is primarily a two-year public community college that awards associate degrees and technical credentials, offers a slate of A.I. certificates , including AI Awareness, AI Practitioner, and a B.S. in Applied Artificial Intelligence. Maricopa Community Colleges offers a B.S. in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning “designed to prepare you for a career in the booming industry of A.I.” These colleges are not approaching A.I. through a prioritization of the “productive struggle” of learning. They are valuing the skill of A.I. fluency as necessary to prepare for a postgraduate career, which is the very point of this kind of institution. Enrollment data shows that students are pursuing their coursework accordingly, as majors in engineering, mechanics, and health care are rising while computer science enrollment declines. This approach maps onto M.I.T.’s framework through its focus on practical application and its total disregard of everything to do with residential experience or research apprenticeship. Large public universities occupy a position similar to M.I.T.’s: Their broad curricula and varied student experiences combine elements of liberal-arts education and career preparation. Arizona State’s push toward A.I.-integrated, work-based curriculum is functionally similar to M.I.T.’s recommendation to expand experimental and project-based learning. Both schools want A.I. to enable students to be more ambitious in their work by cutting out the need to learn foundational technical skills that A.I. is good at, allowing students to focus instead on high-level experimentation and real-world application that would previously have been impossible within an undergraduate schedule. The framing by each school, though, is different: A.S.U.’s is an almost entirely economic reaction to data that shows college-educated young adults are facing high rates of unemployment, while M.I.T.’s frame is human flourishing and intellectual maturity, with employability — while important — secondary. At what point is the attempt moot? It would be so simple if this whole issue could be solved by institutions optimizing their approaches to A.I. policy around whatever they determine they are selling. But each of the many versions of education requires its own approach. While a student working in an engineering lab at M.I.T. probably should use A.I. to expand the possibilities of their studies and contributions to the world, my time as an English major at a liberal-arts college might have been utterly useless if A.I. had been a part of it. A former professor of mine has the same view, and she is approaching her course on writers Herman Melville and Nathaniel Hawthorne by making all assignments handwritten, focusing less on the output and more on process. My sister, a community-college history professor, is allowing her students to use A.I. but requires them to be transparent about their use. She is not giving quizzes or tests and is more heavily weighting their in-class conversations and primary-source analysis. I write this with some feeling of hope that A.I. will make schools confront the mess that education has become, especially in the wake of Covid, as students report higher rates of dissatisfaction and isolation. M.I.T.’s report writes that A.I. “is imposing new pressures on a community still working to restore the foundational habits and attitudes that residential education depends on … A.I. could accelerate this erosion. Or it could be the impetus for a deliberate rebuilding.” If all schools, especially higher education institutions, followed M.I.T.’s prescription to identify their own purposes and design their A.I. policies accordingly, the outcome could be a clear distinction between the kinds of schools that value productive struggle — where those who want to philosophize can go to think and read and discuss — and those that are designed to prepare students for tangible jobs in an evolving workforce. But none of this discussion of A.I. education policy arrives in a vacuum. I imagine that A.I. technology is accelerating more quickly than schools will be able to reach a stable equilibrium. As M.I.T.’s report acknowledges, “A.I. is progressing across almost every domain and on a timescale too compressed for society to properly observe and analyze its impacts and then gradually adapt.” But insofar as the immediate issue is how institutions should approach A.I. in education, this moment begs a welcome re-evaluation of purpose for institutions at every level. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks about the trade war with the United States on August 24, 2026. (Photo by ANDREJ IVANOV / AFP via Getty Images) Donald Trump has plunged the United States into a new and destructive round of the trade war with Canada. Obviously, the U.S.-Canada relationship is a bigger deal for Canada than for the United States since we’re a much larger country with a wider set of global entanglements. But fundamentally, Canada really does matter quite a bit to the United States, probably more than any other single country. And I think Americans — especially anti-Trump Americans — are sleeping on the extent to which this is viewed in Canada as an existential moment. The nature of Trump’s demands, which include things that have long been on the U.S. side of the bilateral-trade docket but also speak to language arrangements that are at the core of Canadian national identity as well as Canada’s basic sovereign right to conduct trade relations with other countries, is stark. And Trump contextualized those demands by snarking that he was going to turn Canada into the 51st state, a “joke” that JD Vance couldn’t help himself but repeat at the height of the crisis. Democrats have uniformly opposed these moves, as far as I can tell, but they’ve hardly risen to meet the moment in a diplomatically or politically sophisticated manner, nor are they genuinely attentive to the dynamics on the Canadian side of the border. Worst of all, Gavin Newsom in an interview with Canadian television committed to dealing with Canada more respectfully but not to reversing the tariffs. This didn’t attract a lot of attention in American circles, but obviously Canadians were paying attention. And their interpretation is that the most prominent anti-Trump figure who bothered to come on Canadian media and discuss this was basically embracing a bipartisan squeeze play to crush Canadian sovereignty. I think the people I quoted above are overreading the level of intentionality in Newsom’s remarks and underrating the extent to which he’s just not very smart. But I also think that Democrats should pay attention to this reaction and do everything in their power to steer away from this dynamic. Trump’s conduct has been truly destructive and shocking to the conscience, and Democrats should say that. For now, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is standing strong. For now, the Canadian people are behind him. And Democrats should say loud and clear that he is right to stand strong and that if they wield power in 2027, they will do whatever they can to roll back this trade war, and if they govern in 2029, they will absolutely end it. Subscribe now Don’t just criticize Trump’s actions — positively repudiate them and promise to reverse them. Do it on Twitter and in the American media, but in Canadian media, too. Newsom is wrong on the politics and wrong on the merits. The strategic logic of vowing to surrender Trump may be deplored abroad, but Democrats should recognize that they’re not as well-liked as they may think. One reason for that is that when Joe Biden was president, he actually didn’t roll back the vast majority of Trump’s tariffs from his previous term. Both Bill Clinton and Barack Obama were broadly free-trade presidents, and free trade is the historic legacy of the Democratic Party from the Jefferson-Jackson era through to F.D.R. and J.F.K. But in the 1970s and 1980s, congressional Democrats became trade-skeptical, and most Democrats in Congress voted against NAFTA and many other modern trade agreements. The Biden administration, which opted essentially for continuity, was sort of paralyzed by its labor union ties from rolling back any of the Trump One tariffs. But while Biden deferred to labor on trade, he did not defer to them on everything — in particular the Keystone XL pipeline. Environmentalists wanted to kill this project, so Biden killed it, even though American building trades and the Canadian government wanted it. None of this is on a par with Trump’s behavior, but it was high-handed and alienating and has made Canadians worry about a good-cop, bad-cop dynamic. But here’s the problem. Trump’s logic is that while a trade war will be bad for 340 million Americans, it will be worse on a per capita basis for 40 million Canadians, so at the end of the day the Canadians will cave. Carney’s contrary logic is that this is an existential threat for Canada and basically pointless from an American perspective. His constituents are willing to pay a price to preserve the True North strong and free, while Trump’s constituents are being asked to take further blows on the cost of living to feed the ego of a corrupt psychotic. Carney’s strategy, though, depends to an extent on his model of the Democrats. If Democrats will surrender in the trade war, then the best strategy for Canada is to stay strong, bear the pain north of the border, inflict pain south of the border, make Trump look bad, and help Democrats win. But if Democrats are just going to play good cop / bad cop, then it raises the question of whether Canada can really hold out forever. If no help is on the way, it might make sense to cave and deliver Trump a big win he can brag about. The need to avoid a hollow victory That’s bad for Democrats. It’s also bad for America. Entrenching the idea that American presidents can make political hay out of bullying friendly countries with negative-sum trade dynamics would be a disaster for American commerce and foreign policy. The United States simply cannot prevail in prolonged geopolitical competition with China unless citizens of other democratic societies sincerely believe that American power is preferable to the Chinese Communist Party. This is something prior American leaders took for granted, but Trump has actually made much of the world prefer Chinese leadership — part of an overall disastrous approach to China policy that is pointlessly obsessed with bilateral export balances rather than the strategic balance of power. Any American administration would try to get some trade concessions from Canada — more access to their markets for our dairy farmers, for example — and that’s totally fine. The fact that countries are friendly doesn’t mean they have no disagreements. And Democrats caring about alliances and international cooperation shouldn’t mean committing to being suckers or to endless free-riding. But there’s genuinely nothing on the U.S.-Canada trade docket that is worth redefining the basic nature of the relationship over. Canada has long been extremely helpful to the United States whenever something really important comes up — from taking in diverted flights on 9/11 to sending troops to Afghanistan, or just the reality that the countries have a cooperative binational electricity grid — and we should act in accordance with that. Today’s post is free to read, but tomorrow’s on the state of fundraising going into the midterms will be for paid subscribers. Upgrade to get the full article tomorrow morning: Subscribe now I don’t think Trump’s bullying approach to trade policy is likely to work, but I also don’t want it to work. If it’s perceived as working, it will be repeated and America will be seen by the world as tyrannizing our neighbors and people everywhere will want to see us brought low. But there’s no need for any of this! Democrats should commit to simply ending the trade war with Canada on a unilateral basis — total surrender — and then reboot discussions after trust and goodwill have been restored. Free trade is a winning issue for Democrats Beyond the specifics of labor union minutiae, I feel like ever since 2016, Democrats have been mindfucked by the idea that Trump protectionism is a stroke of political genius. It’s true that in 2016 he flipped the G.O.P. to anti-trade and he also won the election. That being said, he also flipped the G.O.P. into opposing cuts to Social Security and Medicare! The latter is an unambiguous case of Trump dropping a high-profile unpopular G.O.P. policy commitment. Tariffs, by contrast, are very unpopular : Notably, while free trade is broadly popular with everyone, it’s especially popular with Democratic Socialists of America-curious left-wing insurgents. It’s a free-market idea on the merits, but socialists see it as expressing strong opposition to Trump, and they like it. Here I’ll concede that if you look beyond the Canada situation and consider tariffs writ large, Democrats do face a bit of a conundrum. Democrats tend to spend too much time cooking up “big ideas” and not enough time thinking about priorities. And given that Trump’s overall tariff structure is bringing in a lot of revenue and that the budget deficit is currently something that we should be worried about , ditching the tariffs is yet another promise that Democrats should have to slot in among competing priorities. My pitch for making tariff repeal a major priority is that it hits the quadfecta of being disproportionately progressive, and polling well, and being certified as a good idea by wonkish technocrats, and being welcomed by the business community. I understand that it would be a bitter pill for the advocacy community to pencil this in ahead of a new child-care program or whatever, and certainly it’s less exciting, but excitement is overrated . The other thing I would note is that in budgetary terms, Democrats have grown gun-shy about repealing gimmicky Trump ideas like “no tax on tips.” And I get the caution there. But to say that you need to keep unpopular tariffs because you need the revenue and then refuse to close tax loopholes to raise revenue because you’re worried about opinion blowback doesn’t make sense. There’s no course of action with zero political risk or downside, so given that reality, you might as well make the choice that makes more sense on the merits. The whole fiscal logjam clearly requires some bigger conversations among party stakeholders. The conflict with Canada, though, is easy. Just say no. Share

Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger. (Photo by Win McNamee /Getty Images) Yesterday, I wrote about the distinction between the Insurgent Left and the Progressive Establishment . Today, I want to continue trying to enrich people’s understanding of the Democratic Party factional landscape by drawing a distinction on the moderate side between Tactical Moderates and True Believers. It can be a little hard to tell the difference because if you’re moderate for tactical reasons, you’re of course going to say that you’re a True Believer. And True Believers still believe in the tactical case for moderation and will make that case in an effort to gain support. The distinction is often revealed only in the moment. Abigail Spanberger had a somewhat moderate-ish profile as a House member from a blue-leaning purple district, and she ran for governor of Virginia on that profile and won. Virginia only allows governors to serve one term and is a solidly blue state on the federal level, so to whatever extent Spanberger has ambitions to become a senator or serve on a national ticket or in a cabinet, her incentive is to cater to the Progressive Establishment. The fact that she is instead operating as a force of restraint against the Democratic legislature is thus a source of real frustration to a lot of Virginia Democrats. But I think she’s correct on the merits to raise doubts about mandating collective bargaining for local government employees. When Sarah McBride went on “ The Ezra Klein Show ,” it seemed to me that she was trying to create space for a tactical retreat from an electorally indefensible line on trans women’s participation in competitive women’s sports. Martina Navratilova, by contrast, is trying to persuade Democrats that the left’s line on this is genuinely wrong . I think that within reasonable bounds, tactical moderation is smart. I do not agree with John Bel Edwards’s positions on guns or abortion, but it’s obviously the case that no candidate espousing progressive views on those topics would have won a gubernatorial election in Louisiana. It would’ve been great if he’d been persuaded to run for Senate. In general, I’d love to see Democrats nominate more politicians like that in the Deep South because it would create a chance to make progress on Medicaid expansion. Both parties’ decision to just write off huge swaths of the country as unwinnable is bad for America, and a renewed spirit of tactical moderation would bring real substantive benefits. But I also think moderate Democrats are running on fumes in terms of what tactical moderation can accomplish. Expanding the tent in terms of red state recruiting is a totally reasonable agenda that I think even very left-wing people should see the merits of. At the end of the day, though, if you want to capture the heart of the party, you need to make arguments that are grounded in conviction, and that means arguing on the merits. Subscribe now The Joe Manchin paradox Consider former Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia. Everyone who wasn’t completely addled understood that Democrats were wildly lucky to have a West Virginia Senate seat and that there was no way a conventional progressive could have won the 2012 and 2018 Senate races there. But I think most progressives felt that Manchin was clearly drawing dead in terms of re-election in 2024 and what they wanted him to do in 2021–22 was YOLO it and vote for filibuster abolition and a sweeping progressive agenda. And that really is the logic of tactical moderation. Harry Reid had an old joke about Susan Collins, saying she’ll always be with us except when we need her vote. And there’s clearly something to this. Collins cast a totally inconsequential but highly salient “no” vote on Amy Coney Barrett right before her 2020 re-election, but she cast a consequential vote in favor of Brett Kavanaugh and many lower court judges earlier. She’s criticized or broken with Trump on a number of issues but never really collaborated with Democrats to meaningfully restrain him and clearly maintains a sufficiently cordial relationship with the White House that unlike John Cornyn, she never faced a serious MAGA challenger. But it’s also true that Collins provided decisive votes in favor of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act in 2009, the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, and against Affordable Care Act repeal in 2017. There’s probably just no such thing as a politician who at heart agrees with the base about everything but is also good enough at faking moderation to repeatedly win races in tough states like West Virginia and Maine. So while it’s certainly coherent to appreciate a Manchin-style figure on a purely tactical level without agreeing with him on anything, I think it’s unrealistic to expect that actual politicians are just totally faking it. Among other things, once you start playing the role of “guy who champions the interests of coal communities against the demands of green groups,” you’ll come to realize that the green groups are genuinely wrong about some things. At the end of the day, I think environmentalists are basically right about coal . But no advocacy community is right about everything, and there’s plenty the climate movement gets wrong. Most elected officials are not incentivized to delve too deeply into the merits of policy or to really scrutinize their coalition partners’ demands. But a Democrat from West Virginia is incentivized to find things the Progressive Establishment is wrong about, so over and above anything tactical, he’s likely to find genuine points of disagreement. Personally, I think Manchin was wrong on the merits about some important stuff (notably the filibuster) but also substantially correct that the Build Back Better legislation that congressional leadership was pushing for was inflationary. His push to make Democratic climate efforts more focused on innovation and clean energy deployment and less focused on blocking pipelines was right on the merits. The country would be better off today if Democrats had embraced his permitting legislation more fulsomely. The True Believers All the way at the other end of the spectrum, you have Representative Ed Case of Hawaii. Case is a formidable electoral over-performer. In the Split Ticket database, he overperformed by 17 points in 2018, 14 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022, and 17 points in 2024. He’s been in and out of the Blue Dog caucus over some internecine disputes that I don’t really understand, but he generally has a moderate Blue Dog-ish record. He faced a primary challenge this cycle that, for example, slammed him for supporting the SAVE America Act . The thing about this is that while Case’s vote-getting skills are impressive, there is genuinely no tactical case for having a moderate in this seat. Kamala Harris won his district 62 to 37 . Elizabeth Warren is, as Slow Boring readers know, an absolutely terrible electoral underperformer. It just doesn’t matter because she represents Massachusetts. But Harris did slightly worse in Massachusetts statewide than she did in Case’s district. Case is moderate because it’s what he believes, not because it’s what he needs to believe to win his district. He’s also lost several statewide primaries — once for governor, twice for Senate — in part because the Democratic Party primary voters of Hawaii generally prefer someone more progressive. In that light, it’s actually pretty impressive that he fended off an insurgent challenger this cycle, and it’s notable that he had to do so based purely on arguing the merits with no real electability case to be made. Case is truly a one of one in this regard. But I have absolutely talked to members of Congress who’ve told me they secretly wish they had purple seats so they could mod-out a bit more and then plead electability when the groups give them shit for it. I think this is mostly a mix of lying and self-deception, but it contains a grain of truth. Most people — even people who would describe themselves as quite progressive — have an issue or two where they break from the pack. But vanishingly few safe-seat members are like this. You don’t see many guys in a D+7 seat who espouse an idiosyncratic moderate position on something unless it’s closely related to home state or district politics. But plenty of people have a heterodoxy or two they’re quietly stifling. There are also plenty of members who like to engage in what I’ve termed “ dog-whistle moderation ” or maybe meta-moderation, where they’ll speak in abstract terms about the need to meet voters where they are and change the Democratic Party’s brand and not be held hostage to extremists. Subscribe now These types tend to complain a lot about the Insurgent Left in a way that doesn’t totally make sense. Iowa didn’t flip from being an Obama-Obama state to a Trump-Trump-Trump state because of Bernie Sanders (who, after all, was in the caucus the whole time). It flipped because mainstream Democrats got more left-wing . But if you want to change that, you need less obfuscation and more Ed Case energy. Beyond “the establishment” Mike Zapler wrote a piece for Axios this week titled “ The Democratic Establishment’s Ideas Deficit ” in which he argues that “centrists” know what they’re against but have a harder time defining what they’re for. I think he made some good points but also repeats a fundamental conceptual confusion about this. If by “the Democratic establishment” you mean something like “the party’s congressional leaders and its past few presidential nominees,” then the reason they have a hard time defining what centrist agenda they favor is that they do not favor a centrist agenda. It’s actually not even slightly difficult to specify the policy priorities of the Biden-Harris administration as advanced in Congress by Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. The Biden-Harris administration wanted to increase the tax revenue share of G.D.P. while making the tax code more progressive and to use the vast majority of that new revenue to increase spending on clean energy and social services. They believed in abortion rights and affirmative action in college admissions and a fairly crude approach to elite representational politics. On their watch, domestic oil-and-gas production reached new record levels but only after efforts to halt new leases were blocked in court . They believed in the neo-Brandeisian antitrust agenda and appointed its key leaders to top regulatory jobs. The reason this agenda appears to be just “stuff progressives want, minus some of the stuff that progressives want” is because literally that’s what it is. The establishment’s enthusiasm for progressive policy is tempered by electoral prudence, court losses, and leadership’s need to set priorities, but their agenda is genuinely a subset of the progressive agenda. At the same time, an alternative centrist agenda is not hard to find or hard to understand. It would emphasize deficit reduction to put downward pressure on inflation and interest rates and prioritize clean energy abundance while championing domestic fossil-fuel production as superior to foreign production as long as demand for oil and gas exists. It would center ideas, like performance pay for teachers , that aim to increase the productivity of the public sector. It would be an agenda that balances the need for an inclusive economy with a healthy respect for the virtues of free markets and that takes seriously supply-side regulatory constraints on things like housing and health care . Add in the notions that crime control and border security are genuinely important state functions, not things to be engaged in reluctantly as a rearguard effort to avoid political harm. These are not unfamiliar or secret ideas. They represent substantive moderation, a belief that the progressive NGO blob’s analysis of the major policy problems in American life is not really correct or adequate to the scale of the challenges the country is facing. I understand why many moderate True Believers don’t want to be more assertive about these kinds of issues. They’re afraid of losing primaries to candidates to their left, and they think that articulating some loud and proud moderate positions is risky compared with minimizing the substantive differences and making a tactical case for moderation. That analysis makes sense, to an extent, but I think that after 10 years of factional warfare, we can see that it’s a losing strategy for the long term. Nobody wins elections based on a pure politics of from-the-heart conviction. But opportunism and practicality can’t be your whole argument. Actually picking fights about important public-policy questions — not fights with the far left but fights with the establishment and the status quo — makes you seem more authentic and interesting. Picking these fights could also help push back against the sense that moderates practice an inherently dreary politics of limits and “no, you can’t do that.” I think there’s something genuinely inspiring about an agenda that uses abundant housing, rapid economic growth in blue states, and low crime to unlock new avenues of opportunity. It’s really shameful for New York and California to be worse at teaching kids to read than Mississippi, and it would be really amazing if the results achieved by their public school systems were commensurate with the resources invested. The collective action problem around taking on the groups is real, but a presidential campaign could provide a good context for doing so . Since moderates are better at winning votes, they’ll always have a tactical argument at their disposal. But I think there are a lot of closeted True Believers out there who right now are so afraid of losing to leftists that they forget to actually be different from the leftists they’re afraid of. That needs to change.

(Photo by Erik McGregor /LightRocket via Getty Images) Nate Cohn did an interesting piece about how, personal life aside, Graham Platner was not perceived by voters as especially left-wing — “ Fewer Maine voters thought he was ‘too far to the left’ than said the same of the Democratic Party in general.” This is an important data point, but I also worry that it might get misread. For starters, everything in life is relative. The main point here is that even in a blue state that Kamala Harris won comfortably, the Democratic Party as a whole is seen as too left-wing. At the same time, the party is beset by a leftist insurgency. If people develop the view that elected leftist insurgents will stop Democrats from being viewed as too left-wing, disastrous things could happen. The correct analysis here, I think, is that Platner was well to the left of public opinion on lots of issues — notably trans issues — but so are basically all Democrats. But Platner really did articulate a forceful opposition to assault weapons bans that would put him on the rightward edge of the party. He didn’t do land acknowledgments. He didn’t talk about “birthing people” or BIPOC or Latinx. I don’t think there’s really any evidence that being a white man with tattoos was helping him massively, but these low-effort linguistic cues probably do matter. He did not speak like a person who was constantly worried about aligning himself with the views of left-wing campus activists, and on at least one noteworthy cultural issue — guns — he staked out a moderate position. So I think the moral of the story here is that if you want to be perceived as more moderate, you should adopt some moderate issue positions and talk like a moderate. Mike: I’ve seen a lot of articles framing data center opposition as evidence of strong anti-AI sentiment, but to my eyes, it looks about the same as every other bit of NIMBYism — you regularly see community opposition to solar panels, to utility-scale batteries, to apartment buildings. Do you think there’s really a uniquely anti-AI element to this, or is that just how it’s being read by journalists who are unfamiliar with the broader NIMBY context and also hate AI? It’s a little of both. I don’t think anyone who is familiar with the broad NIMBY context of American life is all that shocked to discover that it is frequently possible to mobilize local opposition to large-scale construction projects. But part of the deal with NIMBYism is that people generally don’t have some kind of big concerns about apartment buildings going up on the other side of the state. That is not in your backyard. My initial read on the whole data center situation was that developers would indeed find that lots of places don’t want these projects, but also that it wouldn’t be a very big deal. There are lots of places in America, and the data centers will just go where people on net decide the tax revenue is worth the hassle. What we’re seeing in terms of political momentum for statewide bans on data centers suggests something broader than a strict backyard-based concern. Most states are pretty big. Why should you care if data centers are going up a four-hour drive from your house? Some of that reflects concerns about electricity prices, which can have less localized impacts. Still, the obvious solution to concerns about electricity prices is just to tighten up the terms on which the permits are issued. Looked at just economically, the obvious rule should be “you can build the data center only if you agree to terms that make it net beneficial to ratepayers.” That may mean a lot of proposed projects don’t get built, or it may mean they get built on terms that are beneficial to ratepayers. A ban doesn’t make sense. So I think you need to bring in the context that people are moderately skeptical of A.I.’s impact on their lives and more skeptical of its impact on society. That really is pretty different from housing. Even real grouchy NIMBY types generally agree that, in principle, it’s good for people to have places to live. So you get a real push and pull of policy. Almost everyone kind of likes the idea of making it easier for young people to afford to buy a place or move into a bigger one and raise a family. Everyone understands why housing is desirable. There is a weird culture of hostility toward “developers” that I think creates a lot of downstream political problems. But even though I’m sure I have tagged people I disagree with as “anti-housing” in the past, I don’t think anyone would characterize their own views in that way. With data centers, though, you have real skepticism that advancing the technology is a good idea. Most people don’t find the “race with China” concept particularly compelling. People worry about technological change costing them or their friends and family a job, and importantly they are not enthusiastic about utopian visions of a post-work future . Source: The Bully Pulpit/Blue Rose Research Now, in response to this polling, A.I. companies have mostly pivoted away from the utopian rhetoric they used to use about this in favor of being more cuddly and reassuring. They now want you to believe that their models will be incredibly useful and productivity-enhancing but in ways that don’t disrupt the labor market, and I’m not sure how coherent that even is. Obviously, there has been a lot of technological innovation over the past 200 years that has not eliminated human labor. But it definitely has eliminated specific jobs or even whole fields or transformed them into barely recognizable versions of themselves or shrunk them. So my broad take is that different kinds of worries are mutually reinforcing. It is hard to build anything in the modern world. A lot of contemporary Westerners have a basically incoherent view by which they are nostalgic for a past era of more rapid change in the physical landscape, and this makes them want to make it illegal to alter the physical landscape, which leads to stagnation outcomes they don’t like, which makes them more nostalgic. But you can find ways to overcome this kind of knee-jerk skepticism about building new stuff. Doing that, though, requires some kind of baseline view that it would be good to have the stuff. With A.I., clearly people have a reasonably strong revealed preference for using it. But their stated views of the technology are pretty skeptical, and they are not especially worried about its progress slowing down as a result of physical construction impediments. The big problem, it seems to me, is that altering the physical location of data centers is actually a very weak lever for making A.I. policy. Even if no data center is ever constructed in Portugal, or wherever, the lives of Portuguese people could be very disrupted by A.I. progress. As such, you need rules addressing both the economic consequences of A.I. and A.I. governance, and neither area can be addressed just with rules about data centers. It did make me wonder how Trump and Mamdani both pair maximalist rhetoric while moderating in practice but also never admitting they’ve conceded an inch. Mamdani dresses up small bore wins as grand socialist achievements, sprinkles in lofty left wing quotations, and throws enough rhetorical chum to his base that nobody dwells too much on the policy. Trump does the right-wing version: quietly retreats, delays, or settles for less, then declares total victory and frames whatever happened as proof that only he could have delivered it. How do self described moderates get out of this unhealthy dynamic and learn the trick? It was more than 16 years ago that my friend Julian Sanchez coined the term “ epistemic closure ” to describe the tendency of a political movement to seal itself off from outside information, a phenomenon he saw at the time on the American right. I think that while all of the trends he identified have gotten worse since then, the left-right gap has also narrowed because you see more and more epistemic closure on the left. The view that all resistance to the policy agenda of green NGOs is driven by fossil fuel propaganda creates this kind of loop where the fact that someone is pushing back shows they are a “shill.” So really obvious counterexamples to the fossil-fuel-propaganda theory of everything don’t get raised or heard, and there’s no actual discussion inside the movement about what the strategic or tactical issues even are. Brown /Contributor via Getty Images) I did a panel with Adam Gray and Tom Suozzi at WelcomeFest where they outlined their Promise to America , an effort to put some meat on the bones of the general idea of moderation. One of the things they say is “we are capitalist, not socialist,” which is definitely a sentiment that I agree with. Suozzi said on the panel, very correctly, that market economies have dramatically outperformed the competition and delivered, while not perfect societies, certainly the greatest levels of material prosperity that we see anywhere on Earth. This is all totally correct, but I think that people who know that it’s correct need to think more about why, despite its correctness, it has become so unfashionable for young people to embrace capitalism. I think one really important reason is that if you look at what people spend money on, you know housing and health care are the two most important sectors by far. Young people consume far below-average amounts of health care, though, meaning that their consumption is really dominated by housing. A large share of the population consumes housing in the form of renting a home from themselves, so they are somewhat insulated from the ups and downs of the housing market. But those people are mostly old. If you’re young, your experience of the economy is dominated by the housing situation. And the housing situation in the United States is not very good. So I think for most young people “capitalism” means something like “the status quo system,” and they perceive the status quo system to be pretty bad because they are super exposed to the single most dysfunctional element of the status quo economic system. Now, in my capacity as a lawyer for capitalism, I am happy to point out that not only is housing the most dysfunctional element of the status quo economy, but it’s also the element that is run in the least capitalistic way . Far and away the number one thing that could improve young people’s living standards in America would be to embrace more market-oriented housing policies. But for anyone to understand that, those inclined to tout the virtues of capitalism need to embrace that idea. As a political pragmatist, I don’t really blame Suozzi for blasting efforts to foist zoning reform on his constituents on Long Island a few years ago since his district is a wretched hive of NIMBYism. But younger people’s lived experience of “capitalism” is of central planning and massive shortages of the single most important item they consume. So of course if people tell them the alternative to the status quo is “socialism,” a lot of them are going to want that. America’s slow-motion housing crisis Of course, on one level, housing in the United States is very capitalistic. The overwhelming majority of it is constructed with private capital and sold or rented for profit. Most homes are also privately owned — mostly by owner-occupants but with a significant sector of small-time landlords and a handful of large-scale ones, too. Public and nonprofit housing do exist in the United States, but they are a relatively small niche. The result is a housing sector awash in private capital and profit-seeking. What it lacks is much in the way of free markets. And these anti-market policies have grown up, over time, in insidious ways and merged to create a situation where, by 2026, we are dealing with systemic housing shortages almost everywhere in the country. This mess all goes back 100 years to the Supreme Court’s Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty decision, which determined that it is perfectly legitimate to make apartment buildings illegal on certain swaths of land. This is just a huge contravention of the basic logic of free enterprise. It’s not that everyone — or even most people, or even a particularly large minority of people — ought to live in multi-family dwellings. But a small apartment on cheap land is an obvious method of housing low-income people, and low-income people need places to live. And where land is expensive , stacking dwellings vertically is the most normal and obvious way to ensure that supply and demand curves can balance out. But widespread midcentury apartment bans did not produce an acute crisis, because of the widespread adoption of the automobile. The fact that it was newly feasible to build much more suburban housing was a huge positive shock to supply in the postwar generation, and that development more than outweighed the impact of bad policy. By the late 1960s, much of this new suburban housing was manufactured homes built in factories. In the 1970s, however, new rules went into effect that greatly restricted manufactured housing . The late 1970s and the 1980s then saw the rise of the “ growth control ” movement in the Northeast and California, which sought to halt suburban sprawl in the name of preserving open space. So by the 1990s, you couldn’t build apartments or manufactured homes on most land, and you couldn’t build suburban sprawl around San Francisco or Los Angeles or New York or Boston. But in most of America, a metro area could grow outward and housing remained relatively affordable. Then, after 2008, a consensus developed that too many people were getting mortgages, so we made it harder to finance new suburban starter homes on top of everything else. For a little while the impact of this wasn’t so notable, but for the past decade or so — since the labor market normalized — we’ve been living in a kind of Everywhere Shortage. My account of the phases of this crisis follows the work of Kevin Erdmann, who calculates that we’re about 15 million total units short . Erdmann was also the first to observe the importance of incorporating events such as the 1970s crackdown on manufactured homes into our understanding of the lead-up to the Great Recession. But the upshot is that we’re in a really bad situation in this country. Share Ideas versus vibes Notably, the people who constructed America’s system of widespread comprehensive central planning of the housing market did not typically think of themselves as socialists. And certainly, the typical suburban homeowner regards it as his God-given right to block new development and change in his neighborhood. If you’re an older, reasonably prosperous homeowner, this bad situation probably doesn’t have a negative impact on you. And you almost certainly don’t think of yourself as a communist who strongly favors central planning and believes free markets are nonsense. If you’re a young person facing higher rents and despairing about getting on the path to homeownership, you probably don’t think of yourself as a victim of a failed socialist economic experiment the way a refugee fleeing Cuba or Venezuela would. The victims of bad housing policy hear people talking about how America is a great free-market success story, so if they feel that the success story is not working for them personally, they conclude that capitalism and free markets are in fact a big failure. I would also note that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act passed with overwhelming bipartisan support, but all of the “no” votes came from Republicans . And what those Republicans were objecting to was not the NEPA waivers, manufactured-home deregulation, or regulatory favors for community banks — it was some fairly small incentives to try to get localities to change their zoning. One of the main reasons that statewide zoning reforms keep failing in the Northeast is that Acela Corridor Republicans oppose them . In Maine and New Hampshire and California, Republicans have seen YIMBYism as a form of deregulation and backed it, so big bills have passed. But in New York and Maryland and New Jersey and Connecticut, they’ve seen it as trampling on the sanctity of local control, and it’s been very hard to get anything done. These are the most invisible people in the discourse relative to their practical significance in American politics. Not just because they directly block housing (though they do block housing), but because politically cautious moderate Democrats fear a backlash from the right if they embrace housing deregulation. Obviously, I do not agree with right-NIMBYs on the merits. But they are important, and I think there is remarkably little engagement with their views. What you tend to get is either name-calling leftists asserting these types are racist, or else Manhattan Institute types rationalizing away the bad behavior of northeastern Republicans. It seems to me, though, that if you want to understand youth socialism, you need to understand why middle-aged and elderly conservatives see opposition to new housing as consistent with their support for capitalism. In their view when you buy a home in a single-family neighborhood, part of what you are buying is the single-familyness of the entire neighborhood. Left-NIMBYs see zoning reform as free-market deregulation, so they are against it. But right-NIMBYs see zoning reform as contravening their property rights, so they are against it. The truth is, this kind of dispute speaks to issues that long predate the whole idea of socialism. It’s an older one about what property rights even are. The war for simple property rights If you go back to the emergence of what we understand as capitalism, the prior system was, of course, not socialism but feudalism. And a key aspect of pre-capitalist property rights is that they tended to be very complicated. In Jane Austen’s Regency-era novels, the characters are constantly grappling with parcels of land that are encumbered by complicated entailments. By our modern lights, the idea that Mr. Bennet could be prohibited from leaving his estate to his daughters is bizarre. It’s either his estate or it’s not. But the traditional mode of thinking was that if an estate is someone’s property, then he has the right to attach whatever kind of stipulation to his property that he wants. When the property is then inherited by someone new, that person inherits the stipulations. To say everyone can do whatever they want with the property that they own would be a major violation of property rights because property rights include the right to impose these irrevocable stipulations. Thinking about it logically, if entailments can attach to a piece of property but can never be removed, then over the long term all property will be encumbered — and over time it will be encumbered by an increasing number of stipulations. Eventually, all commerce will be strangled by the whims of various long-dead previous owners. What happened instead was that over the course of the 19th century, various acts of Parliament restricted entailments. And the whole process of creating capitalism was full of measures like this. Pre-modern property rights were very complicated. People had joint shares in communally owned fields. There were all kinds of complicated partial-use rights to various parcels of land that couldn’t be bought or sold. Simplifying these rights made it much easier to undertake various kinds of transactions and engage in modern commerce and growth. Because the British political system of the time was elite-dominated, this was often done on inequitable terms. But it unleashed a ton of growth and made the vast majority of people better off on average. In the modern world, we have recreated a system of complicated property rights. The conventional understanding is that owning a parcel of residential land gives you extensive authority to veto things that your neighbors might want to do, such as redevelop their parcel as townhouses or a small apartment building. In exchange for getting those rights vis-a-vis your neighbors, you lose the right to do what you want with your own land. The people who like the status quo mostly don’t conceive of it as a statist imposition on their personal property rights; they see it as property rights functioning naturally. And the young renters who are locked out of economic opportunity by the status quo also see this as property rights functioning naturally, and thus they become socialists. But the thing that would solve this problem is not a giant, economically wasteful program of public housing construction. It’s shifting to a regime of simplified property rights where everyone has much less authority over their neighbors’ land and much more authority over their own. Share Capitalism needs boldness and vision On the left, there’s a longstanding view that “abundance” and “YIMBYs” are just sock puppets for billionaires trying to bolster the legitimacy of capitalism. To this I say — if only! It’s genuinely true that it would do enormous good for the interests of America’s billionaires and C.E.O.s to see radical housing reform sweep the country. That’s in part because faster economic growth is good for everyone, including billionaires and C.E.O.s. But it’s mostly because, exactly as the leftists fear, housing abundance (and its natural complements like abundance of transportation and electricity transmission infrastructure) would bolster the legitimacy of capitalism. If “capitalism” meant “a system where demand for housing is met by rising quantities of housing rather than rising prices of housing,” then a lot more people would enjoy capitalism. But in a world where “capitalism” means “policy defers to the most risk-averse incumbent homeowners around,” a lot of people naturally feel that capitalism is not working for them. But YIMBYism is dramatically worse-funded than the various NIMBY community groups that are propped up by mainstream foundations. Businesses lobby furiously on picayune regulations and tax policy matters, but the collective action problem in lobbying for housing reform is hard to overcome. And politically engaged venture capitalists and C.E.O.s are much more inclined to whine on Twitter about anti-capitalism than to cut large checks to the people trying to make capitalism actually work. I can’t think of any examples of someone pumping money into a primary that features a YIMBY Republican state legislator trying to give the boot to a NIMBY incumbent. For all the discussion of these issues over the past few years, there is still remarkably little money going into the relevant advocacy. And this creates a dilemma for moderate Democrats. Part of the point of moderation is to be politically savvy and politically cautious, and obviously calling for large-scale land-use reforms is risky. But another part of the point of moderation is to solve actual problems rather than being trapped by ideological dogmas. It just happens to both be true that capitalism + a welfare state is a much better system than socialism, and also that the economic status quo is not working well for young people. The good news for markets is that the specific thing that’s not working well is housing — and housing is a problem where the solution is more markets. But this is only going to be persuasive if people are willing to say it and really push to do something about it. There is risk in pushing for big change, but there are also clearly a lot of people who are sick of the status quo and eager to see big change. Should that change be socialism? Or should it be solving the problem at hand? I know what I think. Share

(Photo by Grace Cary via Getty Images) Not to be melodramatic, but I really believe the future of American democracy has been hanging in the balance the past few years. January 6, as it played out, was more farce than tragedy. But normally, a president who becomes unpopular and loses power is discredited within his own political party. The fact that Donald Trump was able to survive not only electoral defeat but the specter of a failed putsch was an ominous portent for the country. His ability to recapture the presidential nomination and then recapture the office itself is terrifying. And his second term has been a true “no guardrails” presidency. It’s not that he’s suddenly a political superman who’s capable of anything; he remains quite constrained in his ability to accomplish all kinds of things. But the entire Republican Party has proven, time and again, that it will indulge Trump in essentially limitless levels of inappropriate conduct. We have flagrantly unfit leadership at the F.B.I. We’ve seen repeated purges of senior military commanders. Bill Pulte is not only abusing power at the Federal Housing Finance Agency in previously unthinkable ways, but that willingness to abuse power was essentially his qualification for promotion to serve as director of national intelligence. With his pardons, Trump has made clear that there will be no legal accountability for any crimes conducted by his political allies, and he’s had many appointees across a range of agencies make clear that the White House can and will order prosecutions and regulatory crackdowns on his enemies. The bad news for Americans’ well-being — but good news for the long-term future of the republic — is that Trump also massively fumbled the bag. Rather than following a template for political success that would have allowed him to consolidate power, Trump has chosen overreach in almost every domain. And while his opportunistic promise to deliver a lower price level was never achievable, he was absolutely not forced to exacerbate inflation across multiple dimensions. These were voluntary blunders that have given the opposition a chance to beat him. And the opposition has really needed good luck, because despite widespread alarm about these threats, the entire progressive movement has done less than nothing to respond to them. While a hearty few souls have been organizing No Kings protests, the vast majority of activist energy has gone into a series of blue-on-blue primaries in safe districts, typically pitting an “establishment” politician whose views are already well to the left of the median voter against an insurgent whose views are identical on 90 percent of salient issues but who also says oligarchy and hates Israel. Even outside the circles of hardcore insurgents, the broad left-of-center media has displayed about 1,000 times more curiosity about what it takes to win primary elections in New York City than what it takes to beat Republicans in red-leaning areas. But winning in red-leaning areas is what Democrats need to do. Subscribe now If they can avoid blowing relatively easy races in Maine and Michigan, the decisive Senate race will be in Iowa or Ohio. With the Voting Rights Act gone, Republicans have been able to score a decisive advantage in gerrymandering and skew the House map heavily in favor of Trump, as the Senate already was. Democrats could easily win 52 percent of the vote nationally and see a Republican trifecta confirmed in place — except with Bill Cassidy and Mitch McConnell replaced by MAGA cultists. The actual outlook, though, is better than that. Trump’s blundering and unpopularity, plus some good House and Senate recruiting, have put Democrats in a reasonable position to win. Flipping both houses of Congress — and thus delivering a clear sign to American elites that this is not the time to surrender to authoritarianism — is not the most probable outcome, but it is on the table. To seize this chance, though, requires Trump opponents to focus on the thing that actually matters: not whether safe seat Democrats can be compelled to be even more uncompromising, but whether Democrats can win the key races. The House is the states Democrats have long been favored to flip the House, and their lead in the generic ballot is so large that all the gerrymandering probably won’t make a difference. It is worth flagging, though, that with Virginia Democrats’ effort to gerrymander thrown out by the state’s own court and a bunch of red states in the South unleashing aggressive new gerrymanders thanks to the Supreme Court killing the Voting Rights Act, the landscape is now genuinely quite skewed. It would be historically unusual for an unpopular incumbent to see a big recovery between now and Election Day. But if Republicans can depress the Democrats’ generic ballot edge from its current range of six or seven points to something like four, the G.O.P. could potentially win the House. The big issue here, though, is really 2028. There are basically two things that could happen between this November and the end of the next cycle. First, there are several blue states that are not currently gerrymander-maxed but whose own state rules made it impossible to redraw maps in the time between the Supreme Court’s ruling and Election Day 2026. Over the course of two more years, though, Illinois will almost certainly draw an additional blue seat. New York will likely draw one and perhaps two additional blue seats. Maryland will probably create one. But to get to within striking distance of even, Democrats will also need action from Virginia, Colorado, Minnesota, and Washington state, all of which are less certain for various reasons, including the fact that their ability to act likely depends on the midterms. Slow Boring is working with collaborators on some future donation recommendations that will include strategically targeted state legislative races to try to help with this, so stay tuned! There are also secret stakes in this race where if Bottoms wins, Jon Ossoff can run for president or V.P. without giving away a seat.
