The Alchemy of a Shared Bookshelf I took three books with me when I left home for college. Space was limited in a dorm room; besides, I wanted to travel light. So I selected the best of the best from my personal library. I could have included The Catcher in the Rye, but that would have been obvious, pretentious, and ultimately impossible, since I didn’t own a copy. My personal library was not a collection of books I was assigned to read in high school. It was a collection of books and comics I actually wanted to read. My personal best of the best: No One Gets Out of Here Alive , by Jerry Hopkins. This is a biography of Jim Morrison, the lead singer of The Doors. The book had a number of pictures of Morrison shirtless, just wearing low-cut, hip hugger, leather pants. Of course it made the list. Color Me Beautiful , by Carole Jackson. This was a wildly popular book from the early 1980s that helped women and their gay sons identify their most flattering colors based on their skin tone, hair color, and eye color by categorizing them into four seasonal color palettes: Winter, Spring, Summer, and Autumn. Each season has its own set of colors that are recommended for clothing, makeup, and accessories. My mother had our ‘colors done’ in the early eighties, and if you must know, I am a Low-contrast Winter, while my mother was a High-contrast Winter. That meant we could have easily shared clothes, were it not for the fact that my mother was 5’1”. Carrie , by Stephen King. Carrie is perfect. Period. My copy was so worn it had Scotch tape on the spine to keep it from falling apart and was heavily stained by Hawaiian Tropic suntan oil. Though it wasn’t in my library, I cannot continue without mentioning (in excruciating detail) the importance of the film version of Carrie . It is impossible to improve perfection. Like the word “unique,” it cannot be modified. Perfect is perfect. Period. The 1976 masterpiece Carrie , directed by Brian DePalma, is perfect. Period. Sissy Spacek, as the troubled teen who hits puberty, then decides to set her prom on fire, then flips a red Camaro cartwheel-style until it explodes, killing Nancy Allen and John Travolta, is perfect. Betty Buckley, as the gym teacher with a secret (wink), is perfect. Piper Laurie, as Carrie’s Jesus-obsessed mother with a crucifix kink, is beyond perfect (I broke my own rule). Her portrayal of Margaret White is a kind of perfect that transcends. It’s the kind of role that becomes part of your personality. Well, my personality. I quote one of her lines from the film at least once a day. It helps me remember there is good in a world that sometimes feels like a school gymnasium set ablaze. That felt really good. Thank you. This was my freshman dorm room personal library. No irony or humor; those were the books. I was delighted to discover that my freshman year roommate, Jonathan, brought the best of his personal library too, though he narrowed it down to one book only. The book, again without irony, was Ms. Piggy’s Guide to Life . I wasn’t familiar with the book, though the TV show The Muppets was a favorite of mine. The book gave the library depth, that is obvious. What neither of us knew was that the book would launch an unlikely lifelong friendship. This would surprise you if you were to witness how horrible our introduction was and how much we disliked each other for the first few weeks of school. Before we even met, he decided that I was an airhead from California because I played water polo and liked to lay in the sun (Jonathan had a very fair complexion). He nicknamed me “Thor”, which I mistakenly thought was a compliment. The stereotype and nickname were reinforced when, on orientation day, I went to lunch with Jonathan and his older sister Amy, along with her friend (I want to say) Lizbeth, or something similar. I had never met people like this. They wore black clothes and sported black sunglasses on a 90-degree day (with humidity, which was also completely new to me). They were beautiful, but in a different way than the sun-kissed kids I knew in California. Their skin, like Jonathan’s, suggested they spent most of their time inside, and they smoked a lot of cigarettes. Jonathan dressed in Brooks Brothers shirts, wing tip shoes; the kind of clothes my grandfather wore. But it was chic and very East Coast. I found it fascinating, though it wasn’t a look I could pull off. However, it was their distinctive way of speaking that mostly captured my attention. It was literally a foreign language, a hybrid English-French dialect spoken in such a way that the pitch of their voices rose at the end of each sentence (I later learned this was called “upspeak”). Even more astonishing was the subject they discussed most frequently: the social status and class of other people. The four of us wandered Thayer Street, the commercial drag that cut through the eastern edge of the campus, looking for a place to have lunch. We settled on a little café and got a table outside. Amy and Lizbeth had no interest in me whatsoever. Their attention was solely on Jonathan. They doted on him incessantly, speaking in baby-talk that veered on obscenity. Jonathan simply sat smiling, blushing bright red in contrast to his milky skin. This was turbocharged, fuel-injected cultural shock. Who are these people? Are they my age? Is everyone like this at Brown? I hadn’t met anyone else yet. My stomach dropped and I started to panic. What have I done? I don’t belong here. These are not my people. To make matters worse, oh so much worse, I mispronounced the name of the cheese Boursin, pronouncing it “Borsin.” “Oh great, they have Borsin,” I announced before ordering a pita filled with the creamy, flavorful cheese. Jonathan and his gang found this hilarious and proceeded to mock me for the rest of the meal by mentioning Borsin (pronouncing it as I had) as many times as possible in an attempt to humiliate me on my first day of college, in a place where I knew no one, 2500 miles away from home. It worked, of course. I was despondent. Jonathan and his sister Amy grew up in a small town in Southern New Jersey, not technically a part of France. Not once did the thought cross my mind to make fun of them, though in retrospect I could have pointed out that they were butchering the entire English language by speaking in such an affected way. I’m glad I didn’t because it would have been a suicidal act. They may have been from New Jersey, but their mastery of sarcasm and witty banter would have destroyed me within seconds. Not a great start. How did I get so unlucky as to be assigned this roommate? What would we talk about? How would we sleep in the same room? I wanted a brother, this was something entirely different. I finally figured out why we were assigned roommates. It wasn’t scientific. All the freshmen in our unit had last names starting with A and we were both male. We both indicated an interest in Studio Art in our applications, so it was almost a given that we would be selected to room together. The first few weeks were tense, with growing resentment. But there were signs of hope. I became very homesick about a month into the school year. It was a feeling I had never experienced. I lay in my bed, almost unable to move. I noticed that Jonathan was sleeping most of the time as well, and it occurred to me that he might also be feeling homesick. I had invested a lot of energy reducing him to a stereotype. Yet I couldn’t escape the truth: he was just as much a human being as I was. The turning point came one afternoon after classes finished. I returned to the room and decided that instead of reading Art History, I would visit our personal library. We had no television yet. I picked up Ms. Piggy’s Guide to Life , rolled my eyes, and thought, “What the fuck. I’ll read it.” I found the book surprisingly funny and entertaining. I was almost finished when Jonathan walked through the door. I immediately slammed it closed. “Oh sorry, I was bored and borrowed your book.” “And?” That was all he had to say. I responded, “It’s really good. I’m kind of worshiping Ms. Piggy.” His face softened. A smile appeared. I hadn’t seen one since that lunch on orientation day. “I know! She’s like my life.” He was gushing. I looked at him for a moment and then nervously stated, “You know you’re a High-contrast Winter. Do you know what that is?” We’ve been friends ever since. The magic we build for our children, and what remains after it breaks. The fairy door the at the base of our oak tree Piper sat on her knees in a chair, focused on two little scraps of parchment on the table in front of her, a rainbow of colored pencils scattered about. One was a note left by fairies in our backyard. The other was blank and waiting for her reply. Every time Piper bent over the paper, her hair fell into her eyes. She brushed it back and kept printing in careful block letters. She was writing back. My wife and I stood there watching while she worked. She kept stopping to think, then adding another line. Her tongue pushed out a little when she concentrated. She pressed hard enough with the pencil that the letters had to be visible on the back. She was writing to somebody real. That was plain. That night, after Piper was asleep, Nancy and I stood at the kitchen counter with glitter on our hands and a pile of tiny junk from Michael’s spread out between us trying to decide what Misty, our backyard fairy, should say back, and what gift she should leave for Piper. A bead. A button. A fake jewel. A little earring. Tiny scraps of paper. Tulle. Lace. Little bags. Scissors. Glitter on the laminate, glitter on the faucet, glitter somehow on our shirts. Nancy held up a tiny spoon and asked whether it was the sort of thing Misty would gift. I had no idea, but I nodded anyway, lost in the note Nancy had written in miniature, amazed at how easily her handwriting passed for something from another world. Outside the kitchen door, the old oak stood in the dark, the little wooden fairy door we’d bought at a craft store glued low against the trunk. My wife tied the spoon to the note with a ribbon, propped it against the door, and slipped our daughter’s letter into her pocket. Those nights still sit near the top of the list when I think about being a parent. The first door went into that old oak maybe three feet from the side-yard door off our kitchen, close enough that the kids could discover it when playing the yard, but hidden enough so the discovery felt like theirs. The tree was enormous and older than the house by decades. Maybe a century. Its branches sprawled across most of the yard and down the hill, and its trunk was so thick that a child could easily imagine a world inside. The second door was in the stone wall, half hidden behind tall dry grass just to the left of a rose bush, tucked low in the mulch with a tiny mailbox outside that we found at the craft store. A fairy with a pen pal needs somewhere to receive letters, after all. One fairy door was a surprise. Two was a neighborhood. But Nancy and I were smart enough to stop at two. And we learned that while the fairy in the oak was a homebody, the ones in the wall were frequently on vacation — there are only so many notes a parent can write after all. Piper left letters at both, and the fairy that was home wrote back. We never gave either door an official street number, but they might as well have been 419 and a half and 419 and three-quarters. The fairy door in our garden wall. During that summer, Piper left drawings, coins, marbles, little plastic animals. Anything she cared about enough to give to a small friend she came to love. She asked the fairies about their lives and told them about hers. Misty mattered. Her brother was in the story, too, though not the same way. Piper went all the way in. She named them, wrote to them, worried about them. Max was younger, but somehow more suspicious, which put him in prime position to push on the magic door and see whether it moved. He was, as far as any five-year-old can be, a happy skeptic. At the time, I didn’t think about what any of this meant. Nancy and I didn’t stand at the kitchen counter with glitter on our hands discussing child development projects. We did the types of things parents do all the time. We wanted to make the world bigger for our children, but also small enough that they could matter inside it. It’s part of the job. We make rituals and games. We tell stories and make up fairy tales. We hide eggs. We fill stockings. We don’t always know what lasts and don’t know what will feel magical or foolish. Most of the time we’re just hoping. That, I think, is one of the harder parts of being a parent. You’re always putting things into your kids’ lives without any guarantee of where it lives in them ten years later. Stories and traditions. Rules and responsibilities. Sometimes a tiny brown fairy door glued near the root ball of an oak. At the time, you’re not standing there thinking about the future. You’re thinking about the children in front of you. The one kneeling at oak tree and the other trying to see behind the door. You’re thinking about notes to Misty in careful block letters written at the table where you would later craft the perfect response, sprinkled with pixie dust. Whether you’re trying to make their world larger or warmer, or simply more fun, I’m not sure. But it’s from love. Years later, I was in my office reading an essay by a Substack author named Sophia ( I used to believe in magic ) about growing up with fairies and finding out her mother had been behind them all along. At this time, Piper was two and a half hours away in her first year of college, probably taking notes in her stats class, tongue still poking out in concentration. She was a long way from the girl at our kitchen table with parchment and colored pencils spread out in front of her, but not as far as time would suggest. Then I hit the line in Sophia’s essay where she wrote she had been angry, that she had felt fooled by her mother, and the whole thing came back in a rush. The door in the oak tree. The other one in the stone wall behind the tall grass next to the rose bush. The little mailbox. The glitter near the sink. Piper kneeling by the roots, her note waiting to be answered. And with it came a question I had managed not to ask when the kids were little. What had we actually given her? And I immediately thought about the day the door came off the tree. Max pried it loose. We told him it was sealed by magic, so I don’t know if he expected it to come off or open up. But when Piper ran into the house crying that Max was trying to break the fairy door, I ran outside to find him using a spoon to lever it loose. It came off as I came out, and he held to door up toward me with a mix of shock and pride. The back of the door showed plain wood and glue with no sign of magic or another world. I took the door from Max and told him to go inside. I glued it back on. I made up something about the power of fairy magic, and hoped for the best. After that, Piper wrote another note. Dear fairies, I’m sorry Max broke your door. Love, Piper. This one was all words, no drawings. No hearts. You could see her hope fighting with reality in the note. A child who thought her brother damaged a fairy house sat down and tried to make it right. She wanted the fairies to know she was sorry. She wanted them to read it. She wanted them to know she meant it. She wanted them to be real. But could that magic hold? In hindsight, the door was always going to come off sooner or later. What my wife and I never gave much thought to was what would happen to the magic once the fairies were gone. We never pictured Piper looking back on the notes or the gifts or the apology and feeling stupid for caring that much. We saw the notes as evidence of sincerity, not something she might one day have to laugh off as an embarrassment. Eventually Piper stopped writing the notes and the fairies gave way to other things. Tea parties. Card games. Hide-and-seek. School. Friends. The small, crowded life of a child getting older. For Nancy and me, the transition felt easy enough. We didn’t spend much time wondering what happened to all that feeling when the notes stopped. We certainly didn’t ask whether what we’d given her was more wound than wonder. Then Sophia’s essay raised that same question, years later. She wrote that she felt like a fool when she found out her fairies weren’t real. She had been upset at her mother for a long time, but later came to understand that maybe magic was real all along because of what her mother created and how she made it real. That last part is what I hadn’t thought about. I had no trouble remembering the enchantment, and I still felt the injury, but I never knew whether the injury was the end of it. And that’s the reality of parenting. You’re almost never working with certainty. You’re working with hope and your best judgment, making choices that feel loving in the moment, and trusting time will prove you right. And sometimes you are, but sometimes you’re not. Sometimes something you meant to be magic turns out to be a craft store door glued onto a tree. You don’t always know the impact of your choices. Sophia’s essay put Piper back in front of me. My wife and I had built a world in the yard and watched our daughter step into it. All the way into it. She wrote to the fairies and left them gifts. She wrote to Misty the way you write to somebody you expect to answer. So what had we done? Had we given her a beautiful childhood memory, or had we built an early heartbreak with glitter and ribbon and a glue gun? When I picture Piper at that table, bent over the parchment with her hair falling into her eyes, I don’t think about a child being tricked. I think about a child learning to imagine life on the other side of the door. She wrote to Misty. She left gifts by the roots. When Max broke the door, she sat down and wrote the fairies an apology in careful block letters. I can’t find much wrong in that. But the answer here belongs to Piper. I can tell you what I remember building, what I worried about later, and how I feel about it now. But what it felt like on the other side of that fairy door is hers to say, just as it was Sophia’s. So, I went to my bedroom and opened the little wooden box in my dresser. I pushed aside the bent paper-clip people Max made for me, a couple of Nerf darts long separated from their gun, a beat-up Pokémon card, some frayed ribbons, a few Play-Doh figurines, and, for reasons I still can’t explain, a Ziploc bag full of baby teeth. Near the bottom was a small piece of parchment, the letters in pencil pressed hard enough to be visible on the back. I knew what it was before I unfolded it. I took a picture and sent it to Piper and asked, in the careful, over-serious way a parent asks when they are not quite sure whether they did the right thing, whether making that world for her had felt like magic, or like being fooled. After a few minutes, her answer bubbled up on my screen, and it was simpler than my worry. She remembered it sweetly. She obviously knew plenty of childhood magic was made by adults. Santa. The Easter Bunny. All the little worlds parents build and children enter until they are old enough to see the seams. The fairy doors, to her, were not an injury doused in glitter. They were fun. They were ours. She was glad we put them there. So I sat there alone with the note in my hand and thought about the girl at the table, and the daughter I have now. I thought about the old oak, the stone wall, the little wooden door, the tiny mailbox, the spoon tied on with ribbon, the glitter on the counter, my wife writing in miniature because our daughter believed somebody small and hidden might be glad to find it. And I sat there with the message she just sent, and felt glad she had that world for a while. For a long time, I thought the magic ended when the notes stopped. Now, I know better. The magic never had to end, because it was never the world behind the fairy door, it was that she knew to look for one in the first place. She climbed out of a window at sixteen to marry the man her parents had refused. My grandmother, Antigone. The car smells of cigarettes and four children. It is Sunday morning again, which means all six of us will load ourselves into the car and my father will drive us to my grandmother’s house in Larnaca, on the southeastern coast of Cyprus. My three brothers and I are squashed together in the back seat, each of us fighting for territory. No one wants the middle. The middle belongs to the smallest one, which means it always belongs to me. My father smokes as he drives. The window on his side is rolled down and the cigarette smoke is carried out of the insides of the car. In the winter, the windows stay shut and he smokes anyway. None of us thinks to complain. It is the late seventies, maybe the early eighties, and children breathe in whatever their fathers smoke. The road from Nicosia to Larnaca is straight and flat and uninteresting, and it takes an hour to get there. Every Sunday we pass the same dry fields, the same unfinished buildings just sitting under the searing heat. My brothers fight over a comic book. My mother turns around every so often to tell them to stop. My father drives away with one hand on the wheel, a slight squint in his eyes, and a cigarette dangling between the fingers of the other hand, listening to the crackle of the radio. I’m at the front edge of the seat with my hands holding the sides of my parents’ seats and staring at the road ahead from the windshield. Eventually, the blue of the sea flashes between the bends, and all four of us begin chanting, “There’s the sea! There’s the sea!” When we pull into the yard, the door is open before we are even out of the car. My grandmother is there, waiting with her arms open for our arrival. Her name is Antigone. She lives in a house in Larnaca that the state gave her after the war. The house belonged to a Turkish Cypriot family who was displaced in the other direction in 1974. Somewhere in the north, other families are living in the houses Greek Cypriots left behind. This happened without consent, without agreement. My grandmother carried what she could salvage from her life and made this house hers. She planted trees in the yard and she raised chickens. The house is a very basic one. Across the yard stood a small structure, and that was the bathroom. Inside, the walls are plain. The kitchen is a small room with an old table and a few chairs and a stove that has seen many long winters. Religious icons hang on one wall; such is the usual decoration of every Cypriot grandmother’s house of that generation. There are a couple of framed photographs, her husband and her when they were young with their six children, when everyone was still alive. Her husband died before the war. One of her sons died too, both of them taken by heart attacks in their thirties and forties. By the time she lost her house in Famagusta, she had already lost two of the people that were meant to grow old, there, in that house, beside her. She points to the photographs sometimes when we ask questions, and she tells us stories about what her husband and son were like, in a gentle voice. The dead are in the room and they are loved and they are not weighing it down. She also tells us about her elopement. She is sixteen, or seventeen, or perhaps eighteen; the age changes depending on the telling. Her parents have refused her the man she has chosen. He is from a different village, not the match her parents were imagining for her. She does not accept their refusal. She climbs out of a window to meet him. He is steadying a donkey. She mounts behind him, and they ride fifteen kilometres down the mountain. They don’t come back until they are married. By the time her parents see her again she is my grandfather’s wife, and he is the one she chose, and the choice cannot be undone. She tells this story sitting at the kitchen table, holding our hands or pinching our cheeks, smiling at our faces as we listen. “You are my treasures,” she tells us, “You are beautiful and clever and the most beloved children in the world.” I don’t have to do anything to earn my grandmother’s love. The love is not contingent on the cleanliness of my hair or the quietness of my voice or the tidiness of my room. The love is there, when I walk through the door, it is there while I’m eating, while I’m playing in the yard, it is there when I make a mess, and it is still there when I walk out the door. I am six, or seven, or eight, and I think every grandmother is like this. She is not like every grandmother. In the summers my parents drive me down on a Sunday and pick me up the following Sunday. The mornings begin in the yard. She is already awake before I am. Sometimes I find her in the kitchen having her coffee; other times, she is in the chicken-shed at the back, collecting the eggs the hens have laid during the night. There are five or six chickens inside a wire-mesh coop roofed with corrugated metal. Their enclosure smells of straw and feathers. She lets me go in with her and shows me how to lift a hen gently to see if there is an egg under her. The eggs are warm when you find them, warm in a way eggs from a fridge never are. I carry them out, cupped in my hands, two at a time, as though they are small living creatures. We have them for breakfast, fried in olive oil with bread. The yolks are a deep orange from whatever the chickens feed on in the yard. She pours me a glass of milk and watches me eat with the kind of attention that is the centre of her love. She is not watching to monitor me. Watching me is simply what she most wants to do, so she does it. After breakfast we go to the sea, which is a hundred metres from her front door. We walk down the narrow road, my hand in hers, until it opens onto the beach. The beach is a strip with large, grey pebbles, with no umbrella or kiosk. My grandmother doesn’t know how to swim. She’s a Cypriot woman of her generation who spent the first decades of her life inland and the rest beside the Mediterranean, and nobody ever considered teaching her how to swim. She doesn’t let this stop her. She walks into the sea in her dress. A cotton black dress, falling below her knees, is what she always wears. She doesn’t have a swimming costume. The water creeps slowly up the dress until it reaches her thighs, and there she stops. She stands in the sea with the dress floating around her legs, the saltwater darkens the cotton, while she watches me swim further out and back again toward her. I splash her and she lets me. She laughs and doesn’t make a move to resist my playfulness. When I’m ready to come out she walks out beside me. With our bare feet on the protruding pebbles, we put on our flip flops and go back to the road towards the house. We arrive and she hangs her dripping dress in the yard to dry and changes into another one before she makes lunch. This is a day spent with my grandmother, and there are many like it. They are all roughly the same. Nothing happens in any of them, and that sameness is the gift; there is only a grandmother and a child in a yard with chickens, and the sea down the road. Meals appear at regular hours, and the afternoons pass under the trees she planted to turn a house into a home. She tells me stories about her childhood, her early married life in Varosha, the seafront town of Famagusta, full of people before 1974, hotels along the front, before everything was lost. She tells me about my grandfather and how he made her laugh, how he was young and alive. She tells me about the elopement, again. Then she tells me about the war in 1974, how she packed what she could in a few hours and left, never to return. I don’t remember her telling me that my grandfather fought in Greece during the Second World War. I do remember her telling me that she still has the key to the house in Varosha. No family was ever moved to her house. She tells me how the army put a fence around the town and let no one back, a whole town with no one living in it, the buildings still where their owners left them. These things aren’t told in a sorrowful tone. The losses exist in the narration of her life, but they are not the heart of it. When I’m back home in Nicosia, in my mother’s spotless kitchen, with its angled cushions and sterile floors, I do not consciously compare the two women. I only know that the air feels different in my grandmother’s house, that she says things no one else says to me, and that when I sit at her table, nothing is being asked of me. My mother loves me. I have said this and I will say it again. My mother loves me in the register she has, with meticulous hair, unblemished rooms, driving me to lessons, never saying she is proud. The two women learned different steps to the same dance. What I understood then was that some Sundays we drove to Larnaca and the door opened and the woman who lived inside was excited to see me, and that she said so with words and with the way she watched me eat. That woman gave me something I could not name and could not get anywhere else. She gave it to me freely. From the sea off Protaras, where I sometimes swim these days, I can see Varosha. Ten kilometres across the water the town is still standing, the tall hotels along the coast, and nothing moving. I swim out and look at it. Somewhere inside that silence is my grandmother’s house, behind the fence, and the door her key opened. She is in the sea in her dress. I’m ten metres out, swimming back to her. Her dress is dark with the wet, and her silver hair is uncovered, left to dampen in the salty air. She is squinting at me against the sun. She is, in this moment, exactly herself. She’s the girl who climbed out through a window for love; the woman who buried a husband and a son; the refugee who walked out of Varosha carrying what she could; the old lady who planted trees and raised chickens and stands in the sea in her dress because the sea is there, and she cannot swim, but she will not be kept out of it. She’s also my grandmother. And now she is standing there, watching, waiting for me to swim back to her. Image generated by AI When I was little, I did not live with my parents. The outings I had with my mother once every few months were, back then, the biggest events and the greatest happiness in my life. The day before I was supposed to see her, I would always brag to my friends. And of course I did. New clothes, snacks, school supplies, even toys — she always came with both hands full. Her guilt made sure of it. I still remember the first time she took me to Wolmido, a seaside amusement district near Incheon in South Korea. I was six years old. I wore the new clothes she had bought me, and the new shoes too. I had skipped school that day, and I could not have been happier. A ride on the Disco Pang Pang — a spinning, bouncing carnival ride — and an ice cream were enough to make the day perfect. The next day at school, my mouth would not stop. I bragged and bragged, and before I knew it, the day had flown by. After the last class of the day, I walked home with light steps. On my way home, I cut through an apartment complex. The small playground attached to the complex had only a few pieces of equipment. A slide. Swings. And a seesaw. On that seesaw, its paint peeling and metal rusted, sat a mother, a father, and a child. The child looked about my age. She was looking up at her parents, smiling so brightly, so innocently, as if she knew nothing of the world’s sorrow. I stood there for a while, watching them. Why was it? The special clothes and pretty new shoes I had spent the whole day bragging about suddenly looked so shabby. I could not lift my head. Shame had bent it down. I just stood there, clutching the straps of my schoolbag tightly. I think that was when I first understood what it meant not to have my parents with me. Maybe it was pride. Maybe it was some stubbornness I did not yet know how to name. Instead of going home, my little six-year-old self wandered the streets. The sun went down, and night came. Eventually, I reached a playground in the next neighborhood — a place that felt very, very far away to a six-year-old. At that dark hour, the playground was empty. I set my schoolbag down and climbed, alone, to the top of the jungle gym. As I sat there looking up at the night sky, one heavy star flew down and lodged itself in my heart. When I finally returned home after nine o’clock, I was terribly scolded with a switch. I sobbed and begged for forgiveness, but when the relatives I was living with at the time asked where I had been, I stubbornly refused to answer. I only cried. The switch hurt. But the star lodged in my heart hurt more. More than twenty years have passed since then, but the night sky I saw from the top of that jungle gym remains strangely vivid and cold. Since that night, more stars have flown into my heart. Some came from happiness. Many more came from wounds — sharp and burning when they first arrived. Each one hurt. Each one I learned to carry. And slowly, those stars began to give off a quiet light. Not enough to take the ache away, but enough to see by. Enough, perhaps, to make me a little warmer than I would have been without them. Of all the stars I carry, that first one still burns the brightest. PERSONAL REFLECTION A meditation on duty, heritage, and the walls we build to stay safe Photo by Maria Ilves on Unsplash Friend link here . I live in a cabin. This cabin is built with my thoughts and powered by a Worry Hearth in the middle of its one-room building. This is not a cabin where people retire for pleasure or rest and relaxation. This is a cabin entirely made to imprison, because I am confined by my circumstances — my illness, my filial piety, and my sense of duty to my partner, children, and the home and household we have built together. The foundation of this cabin is built on the way I was brought up. The teachings of Confucius and Daoism form the fabric of how my family took care of their own — 2,500-year-old traditions ingrained into the fibres of our identities, including the importance of ancestral veneration and respecting our elders. This brings a sense of obligation, a paralyzing guilt that will follow if I were to walk away. I told my partner when we married that my parents could come live with us; that was my condition for our marriage. The floors of this cabin are laid with my resilience. I came to this country located halfway around the world from the only home I knew. I was just a kid with one suitcase, armed with my parents’ money and blessings. The smooth floors under my bare feet are reminders of where I came from and the lovely life that I have built with my partner. These floors used to be rough, even sharp; shaped by racism, discrimination, and humiliation. These floors were worn smooth by our sacrifices and determination. The walls of this cabin are built from my sense of obligation to my family. Can I do right by them? Every day, we wash these walls down with rituals — this is the business of living. My health, my caregiving responsibilities to everyone else, whatever leftover time I have, this is mine. Some days I am exhausted mentally by just the completion of this washing. I shouldn’t complain because these are the moments that remind me of my existence — that I still have a heartbeat and that I am healthy enough to care for everyone. Then we move to the Hearth. This Worry Hearth is powered by my anxieties. Every day, there are new things to feed it. I gravitated to a career that allowed for control and organization, so the twigs and logs we throw into this fire are not just about my health, my family, or my career. It is also the worry of how to structure, plan, and organize our lives. I can generate a roaring fire some days from just planning something mundane and inconsequential. The glow from this fire is reflected back on my family as I gaze proudly at them. The roof of this cabin is made from my protective tendencies — the bear parent. If you mess with my family, it’s personal. I don’t like starting a fight, but I will sure help you end it. These protective tendencies, unfortunately, block the stars, preventing my family from growing wings and soaring high. It does, however, keep them safe and takes fuel away from my Worry Hearth. Lastly, the windows. Everyone tells me to have a bucket list. I don’t want one. Instead, I see everyone else’s bucket list through my windows. I am content inside my privileged life, having this little cabin where I can observe vicariously and risk-free. As I watch through these windows, I weave. Using my creativity, I craft tapestries for my walls. I now have more tapestries than can fit on my walls, but I still go on — the process of weaving gives me joy, not the display. So, these tapestries occupy a large box in this cabin, a hidden archive of my imagination. I live in a cabin. This cabin shelters me and provides me with the comfort I need. The warmth I get from my Worry Hearth is not just a source of stress, but a source of energy to keep going. This cabin, completely built by my own thoughts, is not just my prison — it liberates me from the cruel outside world. You can monetize your passion Photo by Steve Johnson on Unsplash For many people, our jobs are not our source of joy and passion. (I mean, mine is today. But it wasn’t always like that.) We do our work, and then we come home and do whatever it is that drives us and fulfills us. We read books, we crochet, we write. That’s a healthy work-life balance. This myth was what I erroneously believed when I finally started taking my passion of writing seriously. I wanted to find time for it; I realized I had to make time for it. I would come home from work and write for half an hour every day before dinner. That didn’t work, so I decided to try getting up half an hour earlier and finding time for writing then. That also didn’t work — I found myself unable to prioritize it, hitting the snooze button instead. I tried different schedules, habit trackers, and methods of finding time in the corners of my day to work on my writing. None of them stuck. The problem was deeper: My energy levels were not conducive to passion projects on the side. Fresh out of grad school, at my first 9–5 job, I found myself shocked by how tired I was. No matter how much I intended to start working on my novel, I’d somehow find myself booting up Sims or scrolling Facebook instead — or just staying asleep. When you’re tired, it’s much, much harder to follow your passion, even if it’s something you love and care about. Creative pursuits require brainpower. If you’re exhausted by your job, it’s just that much harder to make that time. Here’s how I managed to find time for my passion project after all — with some tweaks to the game plan. Find the common ground I thought my job (customer service) and my passion (writing) had nothing in common. I was wrong. Writing is in almost every single job. You write emails, you write Slack messages, you write summaries of projects. All of it is writing. But none of that felt like super creative writing. I wish I could say I forced myself into a solution, but the truth is I stumbled upon an answer by accident one day in my customer service job. I was getting many questions about the same new feature (product recommendations) from our customer base. I had already copy-pasted our corporate jargon answer what felt like a zillion times in Zendesk. Finally, I got fed up and wrote up a more friendly, helpful how-to about the new feature, published it on our company blog, and started linking people to that instead. (That night, I woke up in a cold sweat because my manager had not okayed it — I spoke with her about it the next day and thankfully she was fine with it, but I recommend you confirm with your managers first if it’s OK!) That was just the start — there were many other places my writing passion fit As time went on, I discovered multiple ways to incorporate more writing into my job. I wrote up product launches, FAQs, thought leadership, and even ghostwrote a few LinkedIn posts for our CEO. I pitched my manager on hosting recorded workshops for our customers, too. Ultimately, writing at work didn’t compete at all with my job— it made me better and more effective. And it was fun. I loved thinking about what our customers would likely need, and putting together resources to help them do that. The only surprise was that I pivoted to non-fiction. Though I’d always thought I wanted to be a novelist, and I still do, I found an unexpected joy and love in writing nonfiction Following my passion at work led to a passion-filled job The best part is that finding time for writing at work led me to my current job as a product storyteller at Medium. I spent years creating guides, developing resources, and hosting workshops at my customer support job, as a freelancer, and as a content creator. Ultimately, that experience led me to be uniquely qualified for the job I have now, which I adore. Dodge the issue of monetizing your hobby Another benefit: this approach allows you to avoid the classic burnout of trying to make money from your job. When you love something and try to add a pricetag, it can often drain the passion out of your passion project, bogging you down in the minutiae of trying to run a business or make a buck. But by doing it the other way around — make money by bringing your passion into your day job — you can keep the passion alive. And if you feel it slipping? Scale back and focus on your core duties until you’re ready to pick it back up again. Final thoughts If you’re low on time and struggling to prioritize your writing hobby, find a way to work it into your job. You may be surprised by what doors it opens. P.S. Even if your teams have returned to the office, I’m guessing virtual meetings are still a significant aspect of group collaboration and communication. Sometimes it’s still the best way to gather a distributed team for productive collaboration! Leading through screens is hard work, but getting your tech set-up right is going to make the process infinitely smoother and, more importantly, lead to better results. Over the past six years of facilitating virtual sessions, I’ve learned something important: the quality of a virtual workshop often starts with your setup. When you’re running a virtual session — especially if you’re doing it solo — you’re likely thinking about holding the room, guiding decisions, and keeping people engaged across screens and time zones . It’s not about nailing a Pinterest aesthetic — it’s about having the right tools to lead smoothly and confidently. Here are eight pro-tips that make a huge difference. 1. Dual monitors are a must When you only have one screen, you’re constantly toggling between: The collaboration board Participant reactions The group chat An agenda That friction pulls your attention away from the group. With two monitors, you can do a better job of staying present while also quietly managing the flow behind the scenes. I keep my virtual collaboration tool, like Miro, on the big screen, with the agenda and chat on the second screen. This might seem like a small thing, but it changes everything. 2. Keep participants’ faces visible In a physical space, you can naturally read the room. But virtual facilitation requires us to recreate that awareness intentionally . That’s why I put the toolbar with participant faces at the top of my big monitor, right above the Miro board. This will help you: Read reactions and body language See when someone wants to jump in Notice confusion or hesitation Seeing faces helps you maintain something close to virtual eye contact , which keeps participants engaged and reminds them they’re part of a real conversation, not just another meeting window. 3. Hide self-view if it distracts you Watching yourself can pull your attention into performance mode instead of curiosity mode (more on that, here ). Your job is to guide the conversation, not critique your own facial expressions. Personally, I usually hide my self-view because I feel like it ends up being a distraction and is not helpful for fostering connection and engagement. 4. Use Post-it notes, even during virtual sessions When you’re leading a virtual meeting or workshop, you’re juggling listening with synthesizing, and guiding with capturing. It’s a lot! One thing that can help with this is to use a stack of physical Post-its to: Quickly capture ideas or themes while participants are talking Read them back to the group Confirm alignment Transfer ideas onto the Miro board It’s a simple way to stay mentally organized while conversations move quickly . 5. Keep a few things nearby that help regulate your energy Facilitating a workshop — even a virtual one — takes real energy. I keep a few small things nearby that help me stay centered, like a nice-smelling candle, or a cool stone I can hold during intense discussions. This might sound a little unconventional, but good facilitation is about managing the room’s energy . And that starts with managing your own. When you’re calm and grounded, the group usually follows. 6. Lighting matters more than you think Natural light is great, but it doesn’t always work with desk placement. Good lighting helps in a few ways: Participants can clearly see your expressions You look more present and engaged The overall session feels more professional When your setup looks thoughtful, participants subconsciously feel that the session itself will be thoughtful too . Pro tip: I use Hue lights above and in front of my desk so I can tweak the lighting depending on the time of day. 7. An external camera can make a big difference Being able to position the camera exactly where it works best helps create a more natural conversational angle instead of the classic laptop “looking down at you” view. Right now, I’m using a Logitech MX Brio. The biggest benefit isn’t just image quality, it’s camera placement . Again, it’s a small detail that improves human connection through the screen . 8. Keep your beverages handy This sounds minor, but it prevents those awkward moments where you have to pause the session to get up or reset . I keep my hydration station on the right so it’s easy to sip coffee or water without interrupting the flow of conversation. Small logistics matter when you’re facilitating a room of people whose calendars are tightly packed. Good facilitation is often about creating more ease and preventing tiny disruptions before they happen . Why a Solid Setup Is Worth It You might wonder if all this setup is overkill. But here’s the reality: virtual collaboration already starts with a disadvantage compared to being in the same room. People are distracted. Attention is fragmented. Energy is harder to maintain. A strong facilitation setup helps close that gap and allows you to: Read the room more effectively Guide discussions without fumbling with tools Maintain credibility and presence Respect everyone’s time It’s about creating the conditions for clear thinking, productive collaboration, and forward momentum . And those outcomes are worth a little extra effort before the meeting starts. I’ll leave you with one final thought: wearing the leadership hat and the facilitator hat at the same time is HARD. Leadership requires judgment and direction. Facilitation requires neutrality and mechanics. When one person tackles both simultaneously, progress can suffer. If your sessions feel heavy, unbalanced, or exhausting, it may be a role overload. Check out this post to see why this is so hard, and when you might want to bring in reinforcements. The pain you run from is the very thing trying to set you free Image Source: Getty Images Rain tapped against the window in a rhythm that felt louder than it should. I sat curled in the corner, a mug of half-cooled coffee in my hands, scrolling through my phone. Mostly doomscrolling, if I’m honest. One by one, I skimmed through comments on recent posts. Most were harmless. A few were kind. But then my eyes snagged on a sentence that felt heavier than all the rest. It wasn’t the first mean comment I’ve ever received. And it won’t be the last. We live in a world where people feel free to say whatever they want about you, especially when they can hide behind a screen. Most of the time, I brush it off. I remind myself I’ve done the work. That I know who I am. That I don’t need strangers to validate me. But this one was different. It found me in a vulnerable moment. I was tired, stretched thin and less centered than usual. And in that split second, the words sank deep. They pulled me straight back into old wounds, old stories, old insecurities I thought I’d buried. That’s how triggers work. They don’t knock politely at the door. They break it open. And they don’t care how “tough” you are. My chest tightened. My jaw locked. The words rippled outward, stirring something I thought I had buried years ago. I kept scrolling, pretending I wasn’t bothered, but my body told the truth. My pulse quickened. My mind spun. My coffee went cold in my hands as the comment replayed on loop. And in that quiet room, with nothing but rain for company, I realized that this wasn’t about the comment at all. It was about me. About all the times I had believed I needed to be enough. Thought I had to be seen to be loved. And about the loneliness that said told me maybe I’m still not. I walked across the carpet, tracing the familiar pattern with my eyes, trying to ground myself. I could taste the sharp tang of guilt, the acrid sting of inadequacy. And beneath it all, a deeper ache, one I recognized but had hoped was gone. When the Shadow Whispers Carl Jung said: “Until you make the unconscious conscious, it will direct your life and you will call it fate.” Eckhart Tolle names this the pain-body, an accumulation of unresolved hurt waiting for a match to flare. Rumi poetically reframes the sting as something tender: “The wound is the place where the Light enters you.” What if that tiny fracture in my chest was not evidence of brokenness, but the crack through which something greater might emerge? Into the Wound Let me tell you about how triggers feel. Imagine you’re walking through a dim forest. The path is familiar, the air cool, earthy. You’re steady, present. Suddenly, you step into a patch of quicksand. It’s not deep at first, but you’re sinking. Little by little, panic seeps in. That’s what a trigger does. It drags you into the past, into stories you told yourself a thousand times: I’m not enough. I’m unlovable. I won’t be held. You reel, trying to escape. But the harder you struggle, the deeper you sink. Traditionally, we fall into three scripts: fight, flight, or freeze. We lash out, we avoid, or we collapse inside. In that moment by the window, I wanted to do all three. But instead, as my heart slowed, against my instincts, I paused. I named it: This is shame. I pressed my hand to my chest, as if comforting a child. And I whispered, quiet, shaky, but true “ Thank you”. It felt absurd. Pain doesn’t feel like gratitude. But in that trembling moment, I understood the trigger wasn’t cruelty. It was a calling. A Practice Born from Pain Since then, I’ve woven a ritual into the broken parts of my day. When the hurt arrives: Pause. I stop rushing. I breathe into the tightness. I give myself space to feel. Name it. “This is shame. This is longing. This is fear of rejection.” Trace it. I ask, “Where have I felt this before?” More often than not, it’s childhood. It’s old rejections, repeated stories, unspoken needs. Thank it. “Thank you for showing me what still needs healing.” It’s not denial. It’s wisdom acknowledging its own wounds. Choose again. I respond with softness where I once reacted with armor. I speak softly. I set boundaries kindly. I breathe through the grief. Nothing transforms overnight. But over time, the wound softens. The pain becomes wisdom, the ache becomes awareness. The quicksand loosens its grip. A Lotus Grows in Mud There’s a Buddhist metaphor that teaches us that the lotus grows from the mud yet blooms unafraid. Its beauty is inseparable from the murk. Without the mud, there is no bloom. In my life, the triggers are the mud. The bruises, the voices of fear, the stories I whispered in darkness. And my healing, the flowering of self-compassion, clarity, and peace, only happens when I lean into the mud, instead of running from it. Triggers don’t mean we’re broken. They mean there’s more to heal. They’re not punishments. They’re invitations to softness, to truth, to reclamation. A New Relationship with Pain I will never outgrow triggers. Nor should I. To be human is to carry wounds. But what I’m learning is that I can change my relationship to them. I’ve stopped fighting the cracks in myself. Instead, I kneel before them. I press my palm into the rough edges. I see the child behind the hurt, still needing love. I breathe into the tear. Because that’s where light gets in. So if you feel triggered, tonight, tomorrow morning, in a room where the silence grows teeth, don’t hide from it. Stay. Sit. And ask: “What is this pain trying to teach me?” Let the quiet answer. Let your breath be the bridge. Let the pain be the portal. Because beneath the ache is your teacher. And through the crack, your healing begins. I never dreamed that people would still be discussing my book, One Person/Multiple Careers , nearly 20 years after its publication. The world has changed dramatically since then, but it’s clear that slash careers (e.g. lawyer / artist) are here to stay. Does Your Title Involve This Punctuation Mark? When I wrote the book in 2007, I was consumed by how work was evolving and how we were evolving as a result. People were more openly embracing multiple strands in their working lives. These ‘modern moonlighters’ were claiming their dual or multiple vocations proudly with the use of slashes, often finding cachet in their custom-blended careers. The book grew out of a New York Times story I wrote about Angela Williams, then a lawyer/minister, and Rashid Silvera, a high school teacher/fashion model. Angela summed up her dual identities this way: “I put them in jail in the morning and pray for them at night.” Silvera described racing to a limo after school for fashion shoots. While many teachers are ready to collapse when the bell strikes 3pm, Silvera said he was “filled up with love” from his students. After that article, people flooded me with stories of how their slash-filled working lives provided them with fulfillment and joy. “You’ve put a name to the way I want to live my life,” was a constant refrain. My obsession officially began. The book, which focused on the US, was informed by its moment. People were living longer and working longer, spending years accumulating educational and life experiences before starting families. The internet was making learning more accessible and knowledge and creative work more portable. When you can do website design or freelance IT from a coffee shop, it’s easier to have a second role that’s more location-based, say massage therapy or music, that’s done in real-time collaboration with others. Entrepreneurship was also becoming a national mantra, in what Dan Pink presciently called “Free Agent Nation.” For ages, working people and artists had side jobs to pay the bills (e.g. actor/waiter, artist/taxi driver). At the same time, elites often had multiple professional identities to indulge their passions (e.g. the renaissance approach, the athlete/restaurateur). What felt new was how everyday people were being swept up in the “slash effect.” In 2012, I re-released One Person/Multiple Careers with a new introduction. It was less than two years after a global financial crash and the “ gig economy ” (famously named by Tina Brown in 2009) had taken hold. Slashing became even more prevalent, but now we were slashing to survive rather than to thrive. Lifetime employment was becoming a relic as layoffs and restructurings increased. The idea of having 7–10 (or more!) job shifts during a career was commonly referenced . And slashing had gone global. I started hearing from journalists in Europe, Asia and Australia who started noticing the slash phenomenon in their countries and wanted to hear my take. Nearly two decades later, I have another reason to revisit the slash career. In October, I’ll travel to Paris to speak at the Salon SME , the slasheur confab in France. Thanks to conference creator Alain Bosetti and author Marielle Barbe , the slash language and lifestyle have gone mainstream in France. Bosetti has created a national survey to track those who identify as slasheurs , and the word has been entered into two French dictionaries. I’m eager to learn how slash careers play out differently in a culture with less workcentrism, where education and retraining are affordable, and where health insurance is not the job-lock it is in the U.S. Here are a few other reflections on the evolution of the slash career: New names, same idea . Before slashing, we had portfolio , moonlighters, and polymaths. Hollywood has always had hyphenates. Later came gig workers, side hustlers, multipotentialites , and fractal executives. The latest is the Ampersand Manifesto , a podcast featuring people who have built thriving careers in two or more completely different worlds. My personal favorite is “ slashie ,” a friendlier term than “slash” or “slasher,” which I was using way back when. Slashing is everywhere. On LinkedIn, many now define themselves with slashes (or vertical lines). One common question I used to get was how to show multiple identities online. Today transparency is more accepted. Some employers even encourage it — like asking a staffer who teaches yoga on the weekends to lead a workshop during a staff retreat or a Zoom wellness session during the workday. Platforms like Upwork and Fiverr and the creator economy are the latest tools of the slash life. As workplace futurist Rishad Toboccawalla puts it , we are now in the era of the rise of work and the decline of jobs. Slashing across the life course. After my preoccupation with slash careers, I focused on encore careers — meaningful work in life’s later chapters. In interviews with hundreds of people in encore careers, slashing was ubiquitous. These days my work is all about cogeneration — collaborating across generations to co-create a better world. So I think a lot about life stages. Millennials and GenZ are slashing at high rates (upwards of 50–65% according to various recent surveys ), usually by necessity. As we age, I see my GenXer peers and Boomers weaving together threads from our earlier lives or using earlier skills and vocations for income. Nearly everyone slashes now — though it plays out differently at different life stages. A hedge in uncertain times. AI is posing new threats to employment, especially for entry-level job-seekers, and employers are cautious in many sectors given the uncertain economy. In the U.S., thousands of workers in nonprofits, federal government and academia are now flooding the job market. At the same time, members of Gen Z are no longer willing to “pay their dues” for employers that often view them as disposable. The takeaway: cultivate multiple sources of income, and meaning. Time to value unpaid work . In the original book, I included a chapter on parenting because it is such a strong part of one’s identity. Today I would be more expansive around care roles — whether for elders, romantic partners, or friends. The same goes for other unpaid work like volunteering, activism, nonprofit board service — which are often central to who we are and intimately tied to the paid work we do. All of this was made clear in the pandemic, which caused a world-wide reckoning with how we use and value our time. There’s a reason the phrase “essential work” became part of the vocabulary of work. As I was writing this piece, I hopped onto Instagram for a break and was served this New Yorker humor piece, re-posted from 2018: “Honest Dating Profiles of Punctuation Marks.” Though worth reading in its entirety , of course I jumped right to the entry for the slash which begins “I’m an influencer/entrepreneur/social-media guru/small-business owner/technically unemployed.” You know an idea has gone mainstream when there’s a New Yorker cartoon spoofing it. The sun on the balcony of my little town in the Alps reheats my cold coffee. Being in the presence of these mountains already feels like being with old friends. I know their full names. I have seen them act moody and shy, hide behind a cloth of dense fog, or crave attention by showing off their snowy beauty. I’m here for a writer’s residency for a month. It feels like a clear invitation to, well, write. These words are for you, dear reader. I do, in fact, live inside a postcard. The past months have been full of invitations. Some arrived as intriguing synchronicities, some as gentle intuitive impulses, others as sudden, sharp slaps. Narratives shifted. Certainties melted. People exited my life in dramatic ways, making space for delicious new adventures. A few weeks ago, I wouldn’t have been able to access this perspective — to see the blessing in apparent destruction. To see it as an opportunity to start again, to create on the fertile soil of collapse. And yet, here I am, spiraling again around the wisdom of paradoxes. The deepest heartbreaks alongside the most miraculous openings. Desolation and destruction coexist with vibrant aliveness — seeds sprout after a forest fire. We are capable of breathtaking beauty and atrocious acts. We survive the unthinkable and create beauty with what remains. 𒀭 What would it mean to fully embrace (y)our own contradictions? 𒀭 How do you hold space for the messy wisdom of paradoxes? Maybe these contrasts don’t take away from life’s beauty, but actually expand our capacity to be more present with what’s real. This is what makes us human. Our paradoxical nature is part of being alive. When we accept complexity and messiness — both in ourselves and in others — we begin to relate to life, rather than resist it. Nuance becomes possible. So does deep, lasting change. Still, it’s tempting to wish for a simpler world. I see this impulse everywhere — the desire to make things neat and clear, to sort life into tidy divisions. It’s understandable — simplicity feels safe, coherent, controllable. But these divisions exist only in theory, in the fantasy of control. That’s why I see it as a radical act to celebrate contradictions, to stay with unresolved tension long enough for nuance to emerge, to bloom into something messy, unexpected, true. Only dead things are certain. Everything alive dances in varying degrees of uncertainty. May we enjoy the dance. A crash course for motion design beginners Illustration: thirteen23 One year ago, I knew next to nothing about building motion. It didn’t help that the prospect sounded scary — motion means animating, right? And animating means I have to—what—design across time? I just mastered organizing my Sketch symbols, but okay. After several months of diving headfirst into After Effects (it’s the industry standard for motion graphics), I’m glad to say I’ve learned the ropes of both After Effects and motion design in general. If you’re new to motion design or are looking to add it as another skill in your designer tool belt, these tips can help you master it a little faster. First, think like an engineer The science: Learning how to physically build motion The first step to learning how to build motion is to learn how to speak the language. Some of the technical aspects (and the overwhelmingly dense After Effects interface) became less scary after I familiarized myself with a few key concepts. Easing is the acceleration or deceleration of motion between two key points. “Ease out” refers to motion that decelerates as it reaches its end value and is a common form of easing in UI motion (just ask Google ). Showing an easing curve next to its visible motion (Source: Google Material ) Interpolation is the calculation of values in between starting and ending values. Easing curves affect the interpolation of two key frames. Each of these examples have the same starting and ending values, but because their interpolation is different, the motion between those points differs. (Source: Jeffrey Chou ) Key frames are specific values in time. Key frames are what you create and manipulate in most animation programs. They mark the initial, in-between, and ending states of an object. See those dots at the bottom? Key frame markers! Each of those key frames marks a point in time where the object has a specific set of values. (Source: Nicolas Roard ) And if you’re using After Effects, get used to these bad boys, which represent (A) linear, (B) hold, (C) auto bezier, and (D) easy-ease key frames. Duration is the length of an event from start to finish. In web and app development, this is measured in milliseconds, but in traditional animation tools like After Effects, you may be working with frames per second. For example: Shortest amount of time perceivable by the human eye = ~3 milliseconds Button depress and release upon click = ~9 milliseconds Card expanding upon tap on mobile screen = ~18 milliseconds Parenting is creating object relationships by linking one object’s properties to another’s. Source: UXinMotion.net Now, actually applying these concepts can take a bit more grunt work. After all, you’re working in the fourth dimension! That requires a good deal of planning, structure, and experimenting. For example, if we want to animate a card expanding into a full-page takeover, we have to consider: What do the initial and end states look like? (This is usually solved for in initial static design phases) How soon after user input (click or tap) does the card begin to change scale? Which elements will move continually between states and which will fade in or out? How long does it take for the card to move from its original scale to full size? How will each element’s values change over time? Then think like a designer The art: Understanding motion qualities, principles, and best practices Once you master the technical aspects of building motion, building a successful animation comes down to its mindful application. Luckily, the foundations of designing statically and designing with motion aren’t as different as you may think — there are steps we can take in both processes to support the user or to express a brand language. To get started, answer a few questions: How important is this interaction? When it comes to motion design, less is more. Don’t overwhelm users with too much — they don’t need a loading bar that twists itself into a checkmark then rotates in 3D and shoots confetti from both ends. We can draw just as much attention to important interactions by changing one or two values over time, like a swift change in color and increase in scale. How can this interaction express the brand language? When it comes to expressing brand language, describing motion design is just as important as the words, typography, color, and images we use statically. Motion can be just as expressive as it is functional. If the brand is playful and fun, there may be sharper easing curves and larger shifts in scale. If it’s personal and straightforward, try softer easing curves and shorter, more abrupt moments of motion. Keep experimenting with speed, duration, and easing to see how that affects the motion. You might be surprised how something small can change the feeling of the motion. How can motion help support the user experience? We should also consider the functional purposes of motion. How can motion impact the users’ experience and perception of an interaction? How can we help them know where they’re going? Be mindful of the direction of motion, especially in screen transitions (e.g., if a user clicks a “→” button, the destination screen could move from left to right on top of the current screen.) And, finally, how are all the elements choreographed together? Remember when I said “less is more”? That’s especially important to remember when choreographing motion together. What seemed like an elegant interaction in isolation may be overwhelming in the context of the entire experience. Once you’ve built a sequence of events, it’s best to take a step back and replay it several times to see if and where you can remove complexity. Of course, building motion is much more complex than just answering these four questions, but it’s certainly a great place to start. Luckily, there are other amazing people on the internet who have written extensively on motion design best practices. Here are a few articles I reference often: The ultimate guide to proper use of animation in UX Motion design in digital products: A white paper Creating usability with motion: The UX in motion manifesto How do design systems incorporate motion design? Finally, observe and learn Any successful designer is like a sponge, observing and absorbing the experiences and information around them. Take your new eye for motion into the world. Notice not only the static visual design details, but also how those details change over time. The next time you’re perusing the digital world, keep an eye out for: How long it takes content to load The direction pages move as you navigate further How the motion feels (e.g., bouncy and playful or straightforward and pragmatic) How motion helps you understand where you are in the architecture How content maintains continuity between states?
